school-c6-english-a.title: Class 6 English · Poorvi (Part A: Units 1–3)
school-c6-english-a.description: Class 6 English (Poorvi, NCERT 2024 edition onward), chapter by chapter: reading, theme, vocabulary, grammar and writing, with quizzes and chapter tests. Original explanations — read the texts themselves in your textbook.

courses.title: Ch 1 · A Bottle of Dew (Unit 1: Fables and Folk Tales)
courses.summary: A folk tale about a lazy man who dreams of easy riches and discovers that steady hard work is the real 'magic'. Reading for theme and moral, character traits, vocabulary from the story world, simple past tense, and writing a short moral story.
outcomes: Learners can retell the story in sequence and state its moral
Learners can describe characters using trait words with evidence
Learners can use simple past tense correctly in narration
Learners can write a short folk-style story with a moral

lessons.title: Before you read: folk tales and morals

scenes.text: Every night Nani tells a story that ends with a lesson.
Clever foxes, foolish kings, lazy men and wise sages.
'Why do stories end with a lesson?' asks Tanu.
'So that we remember the lesson longer,' smiles Nani.

steps.title: Folk tales
steps.body: **Folk tales** are old stories passed down by word of mouth in a community. They often have simple characters (a lazy man, a wise sage), magic or surprise, repetition, and a **moral** (a lesson about how to live).

steps.title: Fables vs folk tales
steps.body: A **fable** is a short story, usually with talking animals, that teaches a moral (e.g., the fox and the grapes). A folk tale may have people, animals or magic.

steps.title: Example 1 — finding the moral
steps.body:
Story: An ant stores food all summer; a grasshopper sings. In winter the grasshopper is hungry.

- Moral: **Work today to be ready for tomorrow.**

steps.title: Example 2 — features
steps.body:
In a folk tale, a sage gives a strange task. Which feature is this?

- A **wise helper** setting a **test** — very common in folk tales.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Confusing the moral (lesson) with the summary (what happened).

items.text: Talking animals teaching a short lesson
A village story about a clever farmer passed down orally
A tale of a magic pot told by grandmothers

quiz.why: The correct answer is "a lesson from the story". Lesson. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Folk tales were first passed down …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "orally". Word of mouth. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "talking animals". Animals. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "what happened". Events. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "wise helper or a test". Features. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Reading the story: hard work is the real magic

scenes.text: Rama Natha is lazy and dreams of becoming rich without effort.
A sage tells him a magic potion needs dew collected from banana leaves — many litres of it.
He plants banana trees and works in the fields every day to collect the dew.
Years later, the bananas have made him rich. The real magic was his hard work.

steps.title: Story outline (in our words)
steps.body:
- A lazy man wishes to turn things into gold
- A wise man says it's possible — but the potion needs a large amount of dew from banana leaves that he plants and tends himself
- He works hard for years, planting and caring for banana plants
- Selling bananas, he becomes prosperous; when he finally brings the dew, the sage shows him that his effort had already made him rich
- He learns that **hard work and patience** bring real wealth

steps.title: Character traits
steps.body: At the start: **lazy**, **greedy**, **impatient**. At the end: **hardworking**, **patient**, **wiser**. Traits are shown through actions.

steps.title: Example 1 — evidence
steps.body: Trait: hardworking. Evidence: he rose early every day to tend the plants and collect dew.

steps.title: Example 2 — why the sage used a trick
steps.body: He knew lecturing wouldn't work; giving a task made the man learn by doing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing 'the moral is he became rich' — that's an event; the moral is about effort.

activity.prompt: Put the story events in order.
items: The man dreams of easy riches
A sage describes a potion needing banana-leaf dew
He plants and tends banana trees
He becomes prosperous from selling bananas
He realises hard work was the real magic

quiz.why: The correct answer is "lazy". Start. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The dew had to be collected from …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "banana leaves". Banana leaves. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

options: selling bananas from his hard work
quiz.why: The correct answer is "selling bananas from his hard work". Effort. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "wise". Wise. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

options: Hard work is the real magic
quiz.why: The correct answer is "Hard work is the real magic". Lesson. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Words and grammar: simple past tense

scenes.text: Aman tells the class what he did on Sunday.
'I go to the market' — the teacher smiles and corrects: 'I went.'
Stories about the past need past-tense verbs.
Aman retells it: 'I went, I bought, I came back.'

steps.title: Simple past
steps.body:
Used for actions completed in the past.

- Regular verbs add **-ed**: work → worked, plant → planted, collect → collected
- Irregular verbs change: go → went, become → became, see → saw, tell → told, think → thought, grow → grew
- Negative: did not + base verb (He **did not work**)
- Question: Did + subject + base verb? (**Did** he **work**?)

steps.title: Story vocabulary
steps.body: **sage** (wise person), **potion** (magic drink), **dew** (tiny water drops on leaves in the morning), **prosperous** (rich, successful), **patience** (calmly waiting/continuing)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Change to past: 'He plants banana trees and grows rich.'

- **He planted banana trees and grew rich.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Make negative: 'The man worked hard at first.'

- **The man did not work hard at first.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Did he worked?' ✗ → 'Did he work?' ✓
- 'goed', 'thinked' ✗ → went, thought

activity.text: The sage (tell) ___ him a secret. He (go) ___ to the field every day. The plants (grow) ___ tall.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "collected". -ed. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "became". Irregular. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Did he work hard?". Base verb. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "rich and successful". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

options: water drops on leaves in the morning
quiz.why: The correct answer is "water drops on leaves in the morning". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Teacher announces a class book of moral stories.
Each student must write one in about 120 words.
Riya chooses 'honesty' and invents a boy who returns a lost wallet.
Her story is chosen for the cover page!

steps.title: Plan
steps.body:
- Choose a **moral** first (honesty, kindness, patience, hard work)
- Characters: one main character + a helper or challenge
- Beginning (problem) → middle (attempts) → end (result + lesson)
- Use past tense; add one line of dialogue

steps.title: Model (about 80 words)
steps.body:
**The Patient Gardener**
Meena wanted flowers at once. She dug up her seeds every day to check them. Nothing grew. Her grandfather said, "Plant them and wait." She watered them and waited. After two weeks, tiny green shoots appeared. In a month, her garden was full of marigolds. Meena smiled. *Moral: Good things take time.*

steps.title: Make it lively
steps.body: Use vivid verbs (rushed, whispered), a little dialogue, and a clear ending.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a moral that doesn't match the story.
- Switching between present and past tense.

items: My story has a clear moral
It has a beginning, middle and end
I added at least one line of dialogue

quiz.q: First step in planning a moral story?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "choose the moral". Moral first. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

The correct answer is "fits the story". Fit. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "Both true, R explains A". Purpose. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "patience". Change. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "hardworking". Evidence. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "honesty". Truth. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "a scientific data table". Not typical. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "He planted trees and waited.". Past throughout. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

courses.title: Ch 2 · The Raven and the Fox (poem)
courses.summary: A fable in verse about a clever fox who flatters a raven to make her drop her food. Reading a narrative poem, rhyme and rhythm, the meaning of flattery, adjectives, and writing a fable.
outcomes: Learners can retell the fable and explain its moral about flattery
Learners can identify rhyming words and rhythm in a poem
Learners can use adjectives to describe characters
Learners can tell flattery from honest praise

scenes.text: A raven sits on a branch with a piece of cheese in her beak.
A hungry fox below praises her shiny feathers and 'lovely voice'.
Pleased, the raven opens her beak to sing.
Down falls the cheese — the fox grabs it and runs!

steps.title: The fable (in our words)
steps.body: A raven holds food. A sly fox wants it and **flatters** her, praising her beauty and asking to hear her sing. Proud and pleased, she caws — and drops the food. The fox takes it and tells her not to trust flatterers. This fable is very old and is retold in many languages (it appears in Aesop's fables and was retold in French verse by La Fontaine).

steps.title: Moral
steps.body: **Beware of flatterers** — people who praise you falsely to get something from you.

steps.title: Example 1 — why the fox praised the voice
steps.body: To make her **open her beak**, so the cheese would fall.

steps.title: Example 2 — trait words
steps.body: Fox: **sly, cunning, clever**. Raven: **vain, proud, foolish** (in this moment).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking the moral is 'foxes are bad' — it's about falling for flattery.

statements.s: The fox wanted the raven's food.
The fox praised the raven honestly.
The raven dropped the food when she sang.
The moral is to beware of flatterers.

options: false or excessive praise to gain something
quiz.why: The correct answer is "false or excessive praise to gain something". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "sly". Trait. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The raven dropped the cheese because she …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "opened her beak to sing". Plot. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Beware of flatterers". Lesson. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

options: very old and retold in many languages
quiz.why: The correct answer is "very old and retold in many languages". Origin. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Poetry tools: rhyme, rhythm and stanza

scenes.text: The class claps while reading the poem aloud.
Some lines have a bouncy beat.
Words at line-ends sound alike — 'tree' and 'free'.
Poems are made to be heard!

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
- **Stanza**: a group of lines in a poem (like a paragraph)
- **Rhyme**: words ending with the same sound (beak / speak, tree / me)
- **Rhyme scheme**: pattern of rhymes, written with letters — AABB, ABAB
- **Rhythm**: the beat or flow of the lines
- **Narrative poem**: a poem that tells a story

steps.title: Example 1 — rhyme scheme
steps.body: Lines ending: sky / bright / high / night → sky–high (A), bright–night (B) → **ABAB**.

steps.title: Example 2 — rhyming pairs
steps.body:
Find rhymes: cheese, freeze, crow, below, sing.

- **cheese–freeze**, **crow–below**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking words rhyme because they're spelt alike — 'cough' and 'dough' don't rhyme; 'blue' and 'shoe' do.

quiz.q: A group of lines in a poem?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "stanza". Stanza. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "blue / shoe". Sound. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A poem that tells a story is …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "narrative". Narrative. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "beat or flow". Beat. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "lines 1–2 rhyme, 3–4 rhyme". Pattern. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A new boy praises Kiran's bag a lot — then asks to copy her homework.
Kiran remembers the raven.
She says, 'Thanks — but I can help you understand it instead.'
He agrees, and they study together.

steps.title: Adjectives
steps.body: Words that describe nouns: **sly** fox, **glossy** feathers, **sweet** voice, **hungry** animal. Degrees: sweet – sweeter – sweetest; beautiful – more beautiful – most beautiful.

steps.title: Flattery vs honest praise
steps.body:
- **Honest praise**: true, specific, no hidden aim ('Your drawing's colours are bright and neat').
- **Flattery**: exaggerated and used to get something ('You're the greatest genius ever — give me your notes').

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Pick the adjectives: 'The clever fox looked at the proud black bird.'

- **clever, proud, black**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Correct: 'This is the most sweetest cheese.'

- **This is the sweetest cheese.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Double comparatives: 'more cleverer' ✗ → 'cleverer' or 'more clever'.

items.text: You explained the sum clearly, thank you.
You're the best singer in the world — now give me your chocolate.
Your handwriting has improved this month.
You're so smart, just do my homework.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "sly". Describes fox. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "proudest". -est. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "true and specific". Genuine. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "shiny". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "more beautiful". Long adjectives. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Teacher reads a Panchatantra tale about a monkey and a crocodile.
The clever monkey escapes by thinking fast.
Now the class must write their own fable.
Dev writes about a tortoise who is too proud to listen.

steps.title: Fable recipe
steps.body:
- 2 animal characters with clear traits
- A problem or trick
- A quick ending
- A one-line moral at the end

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
**The Peacock and the Sparrow**
A peacock laughed at a plain sparrow. "Look at my splendid tail!" Rain clouds came. The sparrow flew quickly to her nest, but the peacock's heavy, wet tail kept him stuck in the field, shivering. *Moral: Usefulness matters more than show.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making the story too long; fables are short.
- Forgetting the moral line.

items: Two animal characters with clear traits

courses.title: Ch 3 · Rama to the Rescue
courses.summary: A story in the folk-tales unit about quick thinking and courage in a tricky situation. This course teaches how to read a story for problem and solution, character, sequencing and inference, plus direct and indirect speech basics and writing a short narrative.
outcomes: Learners can identify problem, turning point and solution in a story
Learners can infer feelings and motives from clues
Learners can punctuate direct speech correctly
Learners can write a short story about solving a problem

scenes.text: Kabir's kite is stuck on a high branch.
His little sister cries — it was her birthday gift.
Kabir thinks fast, ties a small stone to a long string and loops it over the branch.
With one gentle tug, the kite floats down. Problem solved!

steps.title: Story structure
steps.body:
- **Problem**: what goes wrong
- **Rising action**: attempts and tension
- **Turning point (climax)**: the key moment
- **Solution (resolution)**: how it ends

As you read the textbook story, mark these four parts in your notebook.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: In the kite story: problem = kite stuck; turning point = stone-and-string idea; solution = kite rescued.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why do readers feel tension in the middle?

- The problem gets harder or time runs out before the turning point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing up the problem with the setting (where/when).

activity.prompt: Order the parts of a story.
items: Turning point — a clever idea or brave act

options: the key moment that changes the situation
quiz.why: The correct answer is "the key moment that changes the situation". Climax. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "how the problem is solved". Ending. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

options: where and when a story happens
quiz.why: The correct answer is "where and when a story happens". Place/time. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "tension". Suspense. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

options: solving a problem or helping someone
quiz.why: The correct answer is "solving a problem or helping someone". Theme. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: 'Her hands trembled as she opened the door.'
The story doesn't say 'she was scared' — but we know.
Readers are detectives who use clues.
That's inference.

steps.title: Inference
steps.body: Working out what the writer suggests but doesn't state, using **clues** + what you already know. Clue words: actions (trembled, grinned), speech, setting details.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
'Ravi slammed his book shut and stomped out.' Feeling?

- **Angry/frustrated**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
'The streets were empty and shops shuttered; only a dog barked.' Time?

- Probably **late at night** or a holiday.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Guessing without evidence — always point to the clue.

activity.prompt: Match the clue to the inference.
pairs: He grinned from ear to ear
She tapped her foot and checked the clock

quiz.why: The correct answer is "clues and prior knowledge". Evidence. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'He couldn't stop yawning.' He is probably …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "sleepy". Clue. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "rainy". Clue. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "quote a clue". Evidence. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "joy". Joy. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Teacher writes: Rama said I will help.
'Where does his speech begin and end?'
Asha adds: Rama said, "I will help."
Speech marks make speech clear.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Put spoken words inside quotation marks: "..."
- Start the speech with a capital letter
- Put a comma before the opening mark after the reporting verb: She said, "Wait here."
- Punctuation of the speech goes inside the closing mark: "Help!" he shouted.
- New speaker → new line

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Punctuate: mother asked where is the key

- **Mother asked, "Where is the key?"**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Punctuate: run shouted the boy

- **"Run!" shouted the boy.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the question mark outside the quotes.
- Missing the comma after 'said'.

activity.prompt: Add the missing punctuation word (type the mark).
activity.text: She said ___ "I am ready." (mark after said) · "Is it time ___" he asked. (mark inside quotes)

options: He said, I can do it.
quiz.why: The correct answer is "He said, "I can do it."". Rules. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "a capital letter". Capital. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

courses.title: Ch 4 · The Unlikely Best Friends (Unit 2: Friendship)
courses.summary: A prose text about a surprising friendship between very different companions. This course builds the theme of friendship across differences, comprehension and comparison skills, words for qualities of friends, and writing a descriptive paragraph.
outcomes: Learners can explain what makes friendships across differences work

story.title: The shelter dog and the cat

scenes.text: At an animal shelter, a big dog and a tiny kitten share a basket.
Visitors are surprised — aren't dogs and cats enemies?
The dog lets the kitten sleep against him every night.
Friends don't have to be alike.

steps.title: Unlikely friendships
steps.body: Real-world examples: animals of different species bonding in sanctuaries, children of different ages or backgrounds becoming close. What matters: **trust, kindness, time together, respect**.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why might an elephant and a dog become friends in a sanctuary?

- Both are social, spend time together, feel safe with each other.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How can two very different classmates become friends?

- Find a shared interest, listen, help each other.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking friends must look, talk or like the same things.

Trust is important in friendship.
Spending time together builds friendship.
Animals of different species can bond.

Left: big, slow, gentle. Right: small, quick, playful.

steps.title: Compare and contrast
steps.body: **Compare** = find similarities; **contrast** = find differences. Signal words: both, also, similarly / but, however, whereas, unlike.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Write a contrast sentence.

- *The elephant is huge, whereas the dog is small.*

steps.title: Example 2

lessons.title: Write a paragraph: my best friend

scenes.text: Nidhi wants to describe her friend Zoya.

She adds two examples of Zoya's kindness.
She ends with what she has learned from her.

steps.title: Paragraph structure
steps.body:
- **Topic sentence**: main idea
- **Supporting sentences**: 2–4 details/examples
- **Concluding sentence**: wraps up

steps.title: Model (about 70 words)
steps.body: *My friend Arjun is the most dependable person I know. When I broke my arm, he carried my bag for a month. He explains maths patiently and never laughs at my mistakes. Though he loves cricket and I love painting, we always find time for each other. Arjun has taught me that true friends are there when it matters.*

courses.title: Ch 5 · A Friend's Prayer (poem)
courses.summary: A poem in the friendship unit expressing hopes and wishes for being a good friend. This course teaches reading a reflective poem, the speaker's voice, imagery, modal verbs for wishes and duties (may, should, will), and writing a short poem or pledge of friendship.
outcomes: Learners can identify the speaker, tone and central idea of a reflective poem
Learners can explain imagery and repetition

scenes.text: Mira writes a card for her friend who is moving away.
'May you find friends as true as you.'
Her friend reads it again and again.
Wishes in poems can say what plain words can't.

steps.title: Reflective poems
steps.body: A **reflective poem** shares the speaker's thoughts, feelings and hopes rather than telling a story. Ask: Who is speaking (the **speaker**)? To whom? What is the **tone** (warm, hopeful, sincere)? What is the **central idea**?

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Line: 'Let me be the hand that helps you rise.' Central idea?

- The speaker wishes to **support** a friend.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Tone of 'I hope I'll always listen when you speak.'

- **Sincere, caring**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Confusing the poet with the speaker; the speaker is the 'I' voice in the poem.

statements.s: A reflective poem mainly shares thoughts and hopes.
Tone means the attitude or feeling of the poem.
The speaker is always the reader.
Central idea is the main message.

scenes.text: 'A friend is a lamp on a stormy night.'
Students close their eyes and picture it.
The poem repeats 'Let me…' at the start of lines.
The repetition makes it sound like a prayer.

steps.title: Imagery
steps.body: Words that create pictures or sensations in the mind (sight, sound, touch): 'a lamp on a stormy night'.

steps.title: Metaphor and simile
steps.body:
- **Simile**: compares using *like/as* — 'as steady as a mountain'
- **Metaphor**: says one thing *is* another — 'a friend is a lamp'

steps.title: Repetition
steps.body: Repeating words or phrases ('Let me … let me …') adds emphasis and rhythm.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Identify: 'Her laugh is music.'

- **Metaphor**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Identify: 'He is as loyal as a dog.'

- **Simile**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling every comparison a simile — only those with like/as are similes.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "like or as". Like/as. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

The correct answer is "pictures in the mind". Images. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "emphasis and rhythm". Effect. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "simile". As. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: may, should, will, can

scenes.text: Class 6B writes rules for being good friends.
'We will listen. We should share. We can help. May we never be unkind.'
Each line uses a helping verb.
These are modal verbs.

steps.title: Modals
steps.body:
- **may**: wish/permission — *May you be happy.* / *May I come in?*
- **should**: duty/advice — *We should keep promises.*
- **will**: promise/future — *I will help you.*
- **can**: ability — *I can carry this.*
- **must**: strong necessity — *We must be honest.*

Modal + base verb (no -s, no to): *She should go* (not 'should goes' / 'should to go').

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'He should helps his friend.'

- **He should help his friend.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Write a wish with 'may'.

- *May our friendship grow stronger every year.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Adding 'to' after modals: 'must to go' ✗.

activity.text: ___ I borrow your pencil? (permission) · We ___ wear seat belts. (strong necessity) · I ___ swim. (ability)

lessons.title: Write a friendship poem or pledge

scenes.text: Zara writes four lines starting 'I will…'

steps.title: How to write (6–8 lines)
steps.body:
- Choose a speaker (I/we) and a friend to address (you)
- Repeat a starting phrase (I will…, May you…)
- Add one simile and one image
- End with a strong wish

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
*I will listen when your day is grey,*
*I will laugh with you when skies are blue,*
*Steady as a banyan, I will stay,*
*May every road bring joy to you.*

courses.title: Ch 6 · The Chair
courses.summary: A prose piece in the friendship unit centred on an ordinary object that carries feelings and relationships. This course builds skills of reading for theme and symbolism, sequencing, describing objects, using prepositions of place, and writing about an object that matters to you.
outcomes: Learners can explain how an object can symbolise a relationship or memory
Learners can sequence events and summarise
Learners can use prepositions of place correctly
Learners can write a descriptive piece about a special object

scenes.text: An old wooden chair stands by the window.
Grandpa sat there every evening, telling stories.
Now, when Kabir sits in it, he remembers those evenings.
An object can hold memories and love.

steps.title: Symbol
steps.body: A **symbol** is an object that stands for an idea or feeling: a chair → memories, belonging, friendship; a lamp → hope. Writers use objects to show relationships without saying everything directly.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
A girl keeps her late friend's bookmark in every book she reads. What does it symbolise?

- **Remembering** and **continuing friendship**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why might a story be named after a chair?

- The chair is central to the characters' feelings or the turning point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Treating symbols as only literal objects — ask what they mean to characters.

activity.prompt: Match the object to what it might symbolise.
pairs: An old chair by the window

options: an object standing for an idea
quiz.why: The correct answer is "an object standing for an idea". Definition. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A title named after an object suggests …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "the object is important". Importance. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "memories and feelings". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "opportunity". Symbol. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "show feelings indirectly". Purpose. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Teacher asks for a summary of a story in 50 words.
Rohan writes 200 words!
He cuts details and keeps only main events.
Now it's 48 words.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body: A **summary** is a short version with only the main events or ideas, in your own words, in order. Leave out minor details, dialogue and examples.

steps.title: Example — summarise
steps.body:
Long: *Meena woke at six, brushed, ate idli, ran to the bus, saw a puppy stuck in a drain, called the guard, they rescued it, she was late but happy.*

Summary: **On her way to school, Meena saw a puppy stuck in a drain and got help to rescue it, arriving late but happy.**

steps.title: Sequence words
steps.body: first, then, next, after that, finally

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Copying sentences from the text.
- Adding your opinion in a summary.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "main events only". Main. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "in your own words". Own words. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "finally". End. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "shorter than the original". Short. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "minor details". Minor. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: The cat is on the chair.
Now it's under the table.
Now behind the sofa!
Prepositions tell us where.

steps.title: Common prepositions
steps.body: in, on, under, over, above, below, beside/next to, between, behind, in front of, near, among, opposite

steps.title: between vs among
steps.body: **between** two (between the chair and the door); **among** many (among the trees).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Choose: The chair is ___ the window and the bed. (between/among)

- **between**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Describe your desk using 3 prepositions.

- *My books are on the desk, my bag is under it, and a lamp stands beside it.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'in the chair' vs 'on the chair' — on a flat seat (stool) usually 'on'; deep armchair 'in'. Both appear; meaning shifts slightly.

activity.text: The cat hid ___ the bed (beneath). The picture hangs ___ the sofa (higher than). She sat ___ her two friends.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "two things". Two. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "in". In. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "many". Many. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'In front of' is the opposite of …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "behind". Opposite. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: 'The lamp is ___ the bed' (at its side)
quiz.why: The correct answer is "beside". Side. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Asha describes her grandmother's shawl.
Its colour, feel and smell of cardamom.
The winter evenings it reminds her of.
Her piece makes readers feel the warmth.

steps.title: Descriptive writing (100–120 words)
steps.body:
- Introduce the object and why it matters
- Describe with senses: look, touch, sound, smell
- Share a memory linked to it
- End with what it means to you

steps.title: Model opening
steps.body: *In the corner of our room stands a chair with a faded green cushion. Its armrest is smooth where Grandpa's hand rested for twenty years…*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Listing features without feelings or memories.

items: I named the object and its importance
I used at least three senses
I used two prepositions of place
I ended with what it means to me

quiz.why: The correct answer is "the senses". Senses. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A memory linked to the object adds …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "feeling". Emotion. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "the shawl smelled of cardamom". Smell. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "what it means to you". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "touch". Touch. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: A symbol is …
questions.why: The correct answer is "an object representing an idea". Symbol. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Preposition for two things?
questions.why: The correct answer is "between". Between. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: A summary keeps …
questions.why: The correct answer is "main points". Main. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'The cat is under the table.' Preposition?
questions.why: The correct answer is "under". Under. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Sequence word for the start?
questions.why: The correct answer is "first". Start. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is a sense detail of sound?
questions.why: The correct answer is "the chair creaked". Sound. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Writers use objects as symbols. Reason (R): Objects can show feelings without stating them directly.
questions.why: The correct answer is "Both true, R explains A". Purpose. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Choose: The house is ___ the school and the park.
questions.why: The correct answer is "between". Two places. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is NOT suitable in a summary?
options: He returned it to its owner.
I think this story is boring.
The boy found a lost dog.
questions.why: The correct answer is "I think this story is boring.". Opinion. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Read: 'Every evening she dusted Grandpa's empty chair and smiled.' The chair likely symbolises …
questions.why: The correct answer is "love and memory". Symbol. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Correct: 'She sat among her two brothers.'
options: She sat between her two brothers.
She sat among her two brother.
questions.why: The correct answer is "She sat between her two brothers.". Between for two. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Best summary of: 'Ravi saved money for months, bought a chair for his grandmother's birthday, and she cried with joy.'
options: Ravi saved up to gift his grandmother a chair, and she was overjoyed.
questions.why: The correct answer is "Ravi saved up to gift his grandmother a chair, and she was overjoyed.". Main idea. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which preposition: 'The bird flew ___ the clouds.' (higher than)
questions.why: The correct answer is "above". Above. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Case: In a story, two friends argue and later fix a broken chair together. The chair could symbolise …
questions.why: The correct answer is "repairing their friendship". Symbol. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which sentence uses three prepositions correctly?
options: The book is on the shelf, beside the lamp, under the clock.
The book in shelf beside lamp clock.
questions.why: The correct answer is "The book is on the shelf, beside the lamp, under the clock.". Correct use. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

courses.note: Plot details of this text are not retold here — read it in your Poorvi textbook. This course builds the theme, reading, vocabulary, grammar and writing skills around it.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Neem Baba (Unit 3: Nurturing Nature)
courses.summary: A text about the neem tree, affectionately called 'Neem Baba', and its many gifts — shade, clean air, twigs for brushing teeth, leaves that keep insects away — and why we must care for trees. Reading for information, personification, nature vocabulary and writing an appeal to save trees.
outcomes: Learners can list uses of the neem tree and why it is valued
Learners can explain personification and why a tree may be called 'Baba'
Learners can use nature vocabulary and compound words
Learners can write a short appeal or poster to protect trees

lessons.title: The gifts of the neem tree

scenes.text: In Nisha's village, an old neem tree shades the courtyard.
Her grandfather breaks a twig to clean his teeth.
Grandma puts dry neem leaves among woollens to keep insects away.
Everyone calls the tree 'Neem Baba' with love.

steps.title: Why neem is valued
steps.body:
- **Shade and cool air**; it grows well in hot, dry places
- Twigs used as **datun** (traditional toothbrush)
- Leaves stored with grains and clothes to keep **insects** away
- Neem oil and extracts used in traditional remedies, soaps and natural pesticides
- Its bitter leaves and flowers appear in some festival foods (e.g., *Ugadi pachadi*)
- India has protected traditional knowledge of neem against foreign patents (a well-known case in the 1990s–2000)

steps.title: Calling a tree 'Baba'
steps.body: **Baba** is a term of respect for an elder. Calling the tree Neem Baba shows **love, respect and gratitude** — as if it were a wise grandparent who gives without asking.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why are neem leaves put in grain bins?

- To **keep insects away** naturally.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give two reasons villages plant neem near homes.

- **Shade** and **insect-repelling** leaves.

steps.title: Traditional uses are part of culture; don't swallow neem oil or give remedies to children without a doctor's advice.
steps.body: General education, not medical advice

activity.prompt: Match the part of the neem to its traditional use.

options: a twig used to clean teeth
quiz.why: The correct answer is "a twig used to clean teeth". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "insects". Repellent. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "respect for an elder". Respect. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "hot, dry places". Hardy. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "natural pesticides and soaps". Use. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: In a story, a tree 'sighs' when the wind blows and 'smiles' at children.
'Trees don't really smile!' laughs Raj.
'It's personification,' explains the teacher.
Giving human qualities to non-human things.

steps.title: Personification
steps.body: Giving human actions or feelings to non-human things: *The neem tree **watched over** the village. The wind **whispered**.* Writers use it to make readers feel close to nature.

steps.title: Nature vocabulary
steps.body: **canopy** (top layer of branches), **sapling** (young tree), **bark**, **roots**, **foliage** (leaves), **shade**, **bitter**, **evergreen** (keeps leaves most of the year), **medicinal**

steps.title: Compound words
steps.body: Two words joined: sun + light = sunlight, tooth + brush = toothbrush, court + yard = courtyard, rain + water = rainwater

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Find the personification: 'The old tree stretched its arms over the sleeping houses.'

- *stretched its arms* (branches) and *sleeping houses*.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Make a compound word with 'tree': tree + top → **treetop**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling every description personification — it must give a human quality.

statements.s: 'The wind whispered' is personification.
'The tree is tall' is personification.
A sapling is a young tree.
'Sunlight' is a compound word.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "human qualities to non-human things". Definition. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "the top layer of branches". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "courtyard". Court + yard. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "personification". Human action. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "leaves". Leaves. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: The class makes a 'tree fact file' for the school library.
They scan the text for facts: height, uses, where it grows.
They organise facts under headings.
A neat fact file helps juniors learn.

steps.title: Skimming and scanning
steps.body:
- **Skim**: read quickly for the main idea (headings, first lines)
- **Scan**: look quickly for a specific fact (a number, a name)

steps.title: Fact vs opinion
steps.body:
- **Fact**: can be checked — *Neem leaves are bitter.*
- **Opinion**: a belief or feeling — *Neem is the most beautiful tree.*

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Scan for the use of neem twigs in this course.

- **Datun (cleaning teeth)**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Fact or opinion: 'Neem trees give shade.'

- **Fact**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Presenting opinions as facts in reports.

items.text: Neem is the best tree in the world.
Neem twigs are used as datun.
Everyone should love neem more than mango.
Neem grows in hot, dry areas.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "looking for a specific fact". Scan. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "the main idea". Skim. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "checked". Verifiable. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "opinion". Feeling. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "facts under headings". Facts. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Write an appeal: save our trees

scenes.text: The eco-club announces a 'Save Trees' poster competition.
Imran draws a big neem with the slogan 'Trees give, let's give back!'
He adds three facts and a call to action.
His poster is displayed at the gate.

steps.title: Appeal/poster format
steps.body:
- Catchy **slogan**
- Short **facts** (2–3)
- **Call to action** (Plant a sapling on your birthday!)
- Organiser's name, date, place (if an event)

steps.title: Model appeal
steps.body:
**SAVE OUR NEIGHBOURHOOD TREES**
Trees give shade, clean air and homes for birds.
One grown tree can cool like several air-conditioners.
👉 Don't cut, plant! Join our sapling drive on Sunday, 9 am, Community Park.
— Eco Club, Class 6

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Too much text on a poster; keep it short and bold.

quiz.q: A call to action tells readers …
quiz.why: The correct answer is "what to do". Action. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "short and clear". Clarity. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "a short catchy phrase". Slogan. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "true". Accuracy. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "date, time, place". Details. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Datun' is a …
questions.why: The correct answer is "twig used for cleaning teeth". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Personification gives …
questions.why: The correct answer is "human qualities to things". Definition. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Baba' is a term of …
questions.why: The correct answer is "respect". Respect. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Neem leaves help keep away …
questions.why: The correct answer is "insects". Use. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Compound word?
questions.why: The correct answer is "rainwater". rain + water. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: A sapling is …
questions.why: The correct answer is "a young tree". Meaning. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Villagers call the tree 'Neem Baba'. Reason (R): They respect it like a caring elder.
questions.why: The correct answer is "Both true, R explains A". Respect. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Fact or opinion: 'Neem trees are the most beautiful.'
questions.why: The correct answer is "opinion". Feeling. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is personification?
options: The old tree watched over the village.
questions.why: The correct answer is "The old tree watched over the village.". Human action. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Scanning is used to …
questions.why: The correct answer is "find a specific fact quickly". Scan. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Read: 'Even in May's heat, the courtyard under the neem stayed cool.' Inference?
questions.why: The correct answer is "The tree gives shade". Inference. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Best slogan for a tree poster?
questions.why: A good poster slogan is short, catchy and positive. 'Trees give, let's give back!' invites people to care for trees, while the others are dull or encourage harm.

questions.q: 'Foliage' means …
questions.why: 'Foliage' is the leaves of a plant or tree taken together. Bark, fruit and roots are other parts of a tree, so they do not fit.

questions.q: Why shouldn't children take neem oil as medicine on their own?
options: It can be harmful; consult a doctor
questions.why: Neem is useful, but taking neem oil by yourself can be harmful, especially for children. A doctor knows the safe use, so always ask an adult and a doctor first.

questions.q: Which sentence has a compound word AND personification?
options: The treetop waved at the passing clouds.
questions.why: 'Treetop' is a compound word (tree + top), and a treetop 'waving at clouds' gives a human action to a non-living thing, which is personification. The other sentences are plain statements.

courses.title: Ch 8 · What a Bird Thought (poem)
courses.summary: A poem in which a young bird thinks its world is first the egg, then the nest, then the leafy tree — until it flies out and discovers how big the world really is. Reading for theme (growing up, widening horizons), stanza progression, rhyme, and writing about how your own world has grown.
outcomes: Learners can explain how the bird's idea of the world changes in each stage
Learners can state the theme of growing understanding
Learners can identify rhyme and stanza patterns
Learners can relate the poem to their own experiences of growing up

scenes.text: Inside the egg, the little bird thinks the world is small, round and pale blue.
After hatching, it thinks the world is a nest of straw.
Peeking out, it thinks the world is made of leaves.
When it flies, it realises the world is far bigger than it ever imagined!

steps.title: Stages (in our words)
steps.body:
- **Egg**: the world seems small, round and made of shell
- **Nest**: the world seems to be the cosy straw nest
- **Leaves/tree**: the world seems to be the leafy branches
- **Flight**: the bird sees the open sky and realises it doesn't yet know how big the world is

steps.title: Theme
steps.body: As we **grow**, our understanding of the world **widens**. What we think is 'everything' may be only a small part. Stay curious and humble.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why did the bird think the world was made of shell?

- That was **all it had seen** so far.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Link to your life.

- A child may think their street is the whole world; school, travel and books show much more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking the bird was 'foolish' — it judged from its experience, like all of us.

activity.prompt: Order the bird's beliefs about the world.
items: The world is a small blue shell
The world is a nest of straw
The world is made of leaves
The world is much bigger than I thought

quiz.q: First, the bird thinks the world is …
quiz.why: At first the bird lives inside its egg, so its whole world is the shell. That is why it first thinks the world is a shell.

options: Our world widens as we grow
quiz.why: The poem shows the bird's idea of the world getting bigger each time it sees more. So the theme is that our world widens as we grow and learn.

quiz.q: The bird learns the truth when it …
quiz.why: The bird learns the truth only when it flies out and sees the wide world itself. Eating, singing or sleeping would not show it anything new.

quiz.q: The bird's ideas were based on …
quiz.why: The bird's ideas came from what it had seen so far, so they were limited by its experience. When it saw more, its ideas changed.
The poem teaches that there is always more to know. So we should stay curious and humble, not stop learning or ignore others.

scenes.text: Students read the poem stanza by stanza.
Each stanza follows a similar pattern: 'I lived…', 'I thought the world…'
Line-ends rhyme in pairs.
Pattern helps show the stages.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Each stanza describes one stage and repeats a similar pattern ('I thought the world was…'). **Repetition** shows the change clearly; the last stanza breaks the pattern with a surprise.

steps.title: Rhyme
steps.body: The poem uses simple rhymes at line-ends (e.g., shell/well, nest/best-type pairs). Find 3 rhyming pairs in your textbook copy.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why repeat 'I thought the world…'?

- To highlight how the belief **changes** each time.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Rhyme scheme of lines ending: small, blue, all, true?

- **ABAB**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Ignoring the last stanza's change in tone — it carries the main message.

quiz.why: Each time a line is repeated, the bird's belief is different. The repetition lets us see how its belief changes from stage to stage.
Each stanza gives one stage of the bird's growing understanding. The whole life is built up across all the stanzas together.
'Small' and 'all' end with the same sound (-all), so they rhyme. 'Sky' and 'ski' only look alike in sound partly, and 'nest/nose' or 'tree/try' do not match fully.
The last stanza gives the surprise: the bird realises the world is far bigger than it thought. That realisation is the poem's climax.
Lines ending small, blue, all, true rhyme as A (small), B (blue), A (all), B (true). That is the pattern ABAB.

scenes.text: In the egg, the bird feels safe and snug.
Seeing leaves, it feels curious.
In flight, it feels amazed and free.
The class lists feeling words for each stage.

steps.title: Feeling words
steps.body: **snug** (warm and cosy), **content** (satisfied), **curious**, **astonished/amazed**, **free**, **humble**

steps.title: Perspective
steps.body: **Perspective** = point of view; how something looks from where you stand. The bird's perspective grows as it moves out.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Use 'snug' in a sentence.

- *The kitten lay snug in the basket.*

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How does perspective change in the poem?

- From inside a shell → nest → tree → open sky.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'Content' (adjective, CON-TENT) means satisfied, different from 'content' (noun) meaning what's inside.

activity.text: Inside the warm egg, the bird felt ___. Peeping at leaves, it grew ___. Flying high, it was ___.

quiz.why: 'Snug' means warm and cosy, like being tucked in a nest. It does not mean tired, angry or cold.
'Perspective' means point of view, the way someone looks at or understands something. A title, stanza or rhyme are parts of a poem, not a viewpoint.
On its first flight the bird sees the wide world and feels amazed. Anger, boredom or sleepiness do not suit such a moment of wonder.
As an adjective, 'content' (said con-TENT) means satisfied or happy with what you have. The noun 'content' (CON-tent) is the list of topics, which is a different use.

options: knows there is more to learn
quiz.why: A humble person knows there is more to learn and does not boast. Being proud, rude or thinking you know everything is the opposite of humble.

lessons.title: Write: how my world has grown

story.title: From my street to the world

scenes.text: At 4, Ravi knew only his home and lane.
At 6, school brought new friends and books.
At 10, a train trip showed him mountains.
At 11, he writes how his world keeps growing.

steps.title: Write 100–120 words
steps.body: Use the poem's pattern: *When I was …, I thought the world was … Then … Now I know …* Add feelings and one surprise.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: *When I was four, I thought the world was our blue door and the mango tree outside. At school, the world became a room full of crayons and new friends. On my first train journey, I saw rivers and hills that never ended. Now I know the world is bigger than any map in my atlas — and I can't wait to explore it.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Listing places without feelings or the 'I thought… now I know…' change.

activity.prompt: Write three stages of how your idea of the world has changed, using 'When I was…, I thought…'.
activity.hint: Think of home, school, a trip, a book or a new friend that changed your view.

quiz.q: The poem's pattern for your writing?
quiz.why: The poem follows the pattern 'When I was..., I thought...', showing earlier beliefs. We can use it to write about how our own ideas changed.
Your piece should show a change in understanding, since that is the poem's main idea. Only places or numbers would miss the theme.
Feelings make writing personal, so the reader connects with you. They are not added just to make it long.

options: Now I know the world is bigger than I imagined.
quiz.why: The poem's theme is that the world is bigger than we first thought. 'Now I know the world is bigger than I imagined' says exactly that, while the others add no idea.
'When I was four...' talks about something that happened before now, so it is in the past tense. 'Was' is a past form.

questions.q: First the bird thinks the world is …
questions.why: At first the bird lives in the egg, so it thinks the whole world is the shell. A nest, tree or sky comes later when it sees more.

questions.q: 'Snug' means …
questions.why: 'Snug' means cosy, warm and comfortable. Wet, angry and cold are not the feeling of being snug.

questions.q: Theme of the poem?
questions.why: The bird's idea of the world grows as it sees and does more. So the theme is that understanding grows with experience.

questions.q: The bird realises the truth when it …
questions.why: The bird sees the truth only when it flies out into the wide world. Eating, singing or sleeping would not show it anything new.

questions.q: Perspective means …
questions.why: 'Perspective' means point of view, the way you see or understand something. It is not a title, verb or rhyme.

questions.q: Which pair rhymes?
questions.why: 'Shell' and 'well' end in the same sound (-ell), so they rhyme. 'Shell/shall' and 'tree/three' differ in the vowel sound, and 'nest/next' ends differently.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The bird's idea of the world kept changing. Reason (R): Each time it saw more of the world.
questions.why: Both statements are true: the bird's idea kept changing, and it changed because the bird saw more each time. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Repetition of 'I thought the world…' helps …
questions.why: Repeating 'I thought the world...' lets us compare each new belief with the one before. This shows the change at each stage.

questions.q: Which feeling fits the final stanza?
questions.why: In the last stanza the bird sees the huge world, so it feels wonder. Boredom, anger or sleepiness do not suit this discovery.

questions.q: Read: 'Inside my little room, I thought the city was quiet.' Later: 'On the rooftop I heard horns for miles.' Theme?
options: Seeing more changes what we believe
questions.why: In both lines a person's belief changes after seeing more: quiet in the room, noisy from the rooftop. So the theme is that seeing more changes what we believe.

questions.q: A humble learner …
options: admits there is more to learn
questions.why: A humble learner accepts that there is more to learn. Stopping reading, mocking others or claiming to know everything shows pride.

questions.q: Rhyme scheme of lines ending: nest, tree, best, free?
questions.why: Nest and best rhyme (A), tree and free rhyme (B), so the lines go A B A B. Rhymes alternate, not in pairs side by side.

questions.q: Which line best shows widening perspective?
options: The world was bigger than the shell had told me.
questions.why: This line says the world was bigger than the shell had told the bird, which shows its view widening. The other lines just describe things without a change in view.

questions.q: Case: A girl from a village visits a big library and is amazed by the number of books. Which poem idea matches?
options: Our world grows as we explore
questions.why: The girl's idea of books grows after she sees the big library, just as the bird's idea of the world grows when it flies. So 'our world grows as we explore' matches.

questions.q: Why does the poem end with flight?
options: Flight shows freedom and the vast world beyond what was known
questions.why: Flight shows freedom and a huge world beyond what the bird knew, so it is a fitting end. The ending is for meaning, not just rhyme or time of day.

courses.title: Ch 9 · Spices that Heal Us
courses.summary: A text about common Indian kitchen spices — turmeric, ginger, black pepper, cumin, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, ajwain — and how they have been used traditionally for health and flavour. Reading informational text, nouns for kitchen items, countable and uncountable nouns, and writing instructions/a recipe.
outcomes: Learners can name common spices and their traditional uses
Learners can tell traditional belief from scientific evidence and know when to see a doctor
Learners can use countable and uncountable nouns with some/any/much/many
Learners can write clear step-by-step instructions

scenes.text: Dadi opens her round steel masala dabba.
'Haldi for colour and healing, jeera for digestion, laung for toothache…'
When Sonu had a cold, she made ginger-tulsi tea.
Spices carry flavour, memories and traditional knowledge.

steps.title: Common spices and traditional uses
steps.body:
- **Turmeric (haldi)**: colour and flavour; traditionally used in haldi-milk and on small cuts; its compound **curcumin** is studied by scientists
- **Ginger (adrak)**: tea for colds and nausea
- **Black pepper (kali mirch)**: flavour; often added with turmeric
- **Cumin (jeera)**, **ajwain**, **fennel (saunf)**: traditionally for digestion
- **Cloves (laung)**: traditionally for toothache
- **Cardamom (elaichi)**, **cinnamon (dalchini)**: flavour in tea and sweets

India's Malabar coast has been famous for spices like pepper for over two thousand years; spices drew traders from far lands.

steps.title: Wise use
steps.body: Spices in food are generally safe in normal amounts. They are **not a replacement for medicine** — for fever, pain or illness that lasts, see a doctor. General education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which spice is traditionally used for toothache?

- **Cloves**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why did traders come to India's Malabar coast?

- For **spices**, especially black pepper.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Believing 'natural' always means 'safe in any amount'.

activity.prompt: Match the spice to its traditional use.

quiz.why: Haldi is the Hindi name for turmeric, the yellow spice. Pepper, ginger and cumin have different Hindi names.
Laung is the Hindi word for clove, a small dried flower bud used as a spice. Cardamom, fennel and cinnamon have other names.
The Malabar coast in Kerala is well known for black pepper. Apples, wheat and tea are grown in other kinds of places.

quiz.q: If a fever lasts, you should …
quiz.why: A fever that does not go away may mean a real illness, so you must see a doctor. Spices alone are not enough, and ignoring it is unsafe.
Curcumin is the natural compound found in turmeric, which gives it its yellow colour. Rice, sugar and salt do not contain it.

scenes.text: Mother says: 'Get some cardamom pods, a little turmeric, and two lemons.'
Ravi asks: 'How many turmeric?'
'You can't count turmeric powder — say how much!'
He learns countable vs uncountable nouns.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- **Countable**: can be counted — a lemon, two cloves, five pods (singular/plural)
- **Uncountable**: can't be counted as separate items — turmeric (powder), water, salt, sugar, milk, rice, advice, information
- Use **many** with countable, **much** with uncountable; **some/any/a lot of** with both
- Measure uncountables: a spoon of salt, a cup of milk, a pinch of pepper

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'How much cloves do you need?'

- **How many cloves do you need?**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Correct: 'Add two salts.'

- **Add two pinches of salt.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'informations', 'advices' ✗ → information, advice

quiz.why: An uncountable noun cannot be counted one by one, and sugar is a mass of tiny grains. We can count lemons, cups and pods.
Milk is uncountable, so we say 'how much' and use no plural -s. 'How many' is for countable things.
Salt is uncountable, so we use a measure word like 'a pinch of'. 'A salt', 'two salts' and 'many salt' are wrong.
'Information' is uncountable, so it has no plural form. 'Informations' is incorrect.
Cloves can be counted, so we use 'many' with them. 'Much' and 'a little' go with uncountable nouns.

lessons.title: Reading informational text: headings and features

story.title: Making sense of a fact page

scenes.text: A page on spices has a title, headings, bold words and a picture with a caption.
Teacher shows how to use them to find information fast.
Students find 'uses of ginger' in 10 seconds.
Text features are signposts.

steps.title: Text features
steps.body: **Title**, **headings/subheadings**, **bold words** (key terms), **pictures and captions**, **bullet points**, **tables**, **glossary**. Use them to predict and locate information.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Where would you look for the meaning of 'curcumin'?

- The **glossary** or the bold word's explanation.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How would you find 'spices for digestion' quickly?

- Scan **headings** and **bullet points**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Ignoring captions — they often hold key facts.

statements.s: Headings help locate information quickly.
A glossary explains key words.
Captions are never useful.
Bold words often mark key terms.

quiz.why: A caption is a short text under or near a picture that explains it. A heading is a title, and a chapter is a long section.
A glossary is a list of words with their meanings, usually at the end of a book. It does not contain exercises or maps.
Bullet points present a list of short points clearly. They are not used for stories, dialogue or poems.

quiz.q: Best way to find a fact fast?
quiz.why: Scanning headings helps you quickly find the part with the fact you need. Reading every word takes long and guessing may be wrong.
Informational texts are written to give facts and explain things. They are not meant to confuse or scare readers.

scenes.text: Sana wants to write how Dadi makes ginger-tulsi tea.
She lists ingredients, then numbered steps.
Each step starts with a verb: boil, add, strain.
Her cousin follows it perfectly.

steps.title: Instructions format
steps.body:
- **Title**
- **Ingredients/materials** (with quantities)
- **Numbered steps** in order, each starting with an **imperative verb** (Boil, Add, Stir, Strain)
- **Safety tip** (Ask an adult when using the stove)

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
**Ginger-Tulsi Tea (2 cups)**
Ingredients: 2 cups water, 1 small piece ginger (crushed), 5 tulsi leaves, 1 tsp tea leaves, sugar/jaggery to taste, milk (optional)
1. Boil the water.
2. Add ginger and tulsi; simmer for 3 minutes.
3. Add tea leaves and boil 1 minute.
4. Add milk and sugar if you like.
5. Strain and serve hot.
⚠️ Ask an adult to help with the stove.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Steps out of order or missing quantities.

activity.prompt: Put the tea steps in order.
items: Add ginger and tulsi and simmer
Add milk and sugar if wanted

quiz.why: Instructions tell the reader what to do, so each step starts with a command verb, called an imperative, like 'Stir'. A question or name does not give an order.
A list of ingredients should state quantities, like 2 cups or a pinch, so the recipe works. Opinions or stories do not help in cooking.
Steps are numbered and in order, because doing them in a different order could spoil the result. They are not random or optional.
The imperative is the base form of the verb, as in 'Stir'. 'Stirred', 'stirs' and 'stirring' are not commands.

quiz.q: A safety tip for children cooking?
options: Ask an adult for help with the stove
quiz.why: The stove can burn you, so children should ask an adult for help. Using it alone, running or touching hot pans is unsafe.

questions.q: Haldi is …
questions.why: Haldi is the Hindi name for turmeric. Pepper, clove and ginger are different spices.

questions.q: Uncountable noun?
questions.why: Water is uncountable because we measure it, not count it one by one. Lemons, cloves and cups can be counted.

questions.q: Instructions use …
questions.why: Instructions use imperative verbs, which are commands like 'Add' or 'Stir'. They are not written as rhymes or past tense.

questions.q: 'How ___ salt?'
questions.why: Salt is uncountable, so we ask 'how much salt'. 'Many', 'few' and 'several' are for countable nouns.

questions.q: Cloves are traditionally used for …
questions.why: Cloves are traditionally used to ease toothache. They are not used for sleep, eyesight or hair colour.

questions.q: A glossary gives …
questions.why: A glossary gives the meanings of words used in the text. It is not a map or an answer key.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Spices are not a replacement for medicine. Reason (R): Serious or lasting illness needs a doctor.
questions.why: Both are true: spices are not a replacement for medicine, because serious or lasting illness needs a doctor. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Correct:
questions.why: Cardamom pods can be counted, so we use 'how many'. 'How much' is for uncountable nouns, and 'turmeric' is uncountable.

questions.q: Malabar coast is famous for …
questions.why: The Malabar coast in Kerala is famous for black pepper. Apples and wheat grow in cooler or drier regions.

questions.q: Which is an imperative?
questions.why: An imperative is a command, and 'Add a pinch of salt.' tells someone what to do. The others are statements or questions.

questions.q: Read: 'Ajwain water is a common home remedy for indigestion in many Indian homes.' This is …
options: a proven cure for all illness
questions.why: The line states that people traditionally use ajwain water for indigestion. It does not claim a proven cure for everything, so it is a statement of traditional use.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'She gave me many advices.'
options: She gave me a lot of advice.
questions.why: 'Advice' is uncountable, so 'many advices' is wrong. 'A lot of advice' is correct.

questions.q: Which instruction is clearest?
options: Boil some water for a while.
Boil 2 cups of water for 3 minutes.
questions.why: A clear instruction gives exact amounts and time: '2 cups of water for 3 minutes'. 'Some water for a while' is vague.

questions.q: Case: A friend says, 'Turmeric cures everything, so I won't see a doctor for my high fever.' Best reply?
options: Spices are good in food, but please see a doctor for a high fever
questions.why: Spices are fine in food, but a high fever needs a doctor. Skipping the doctor could be dangerous, so the kind and safe reply is to advise seeing one.

questions.q: Measure word for an uncountable noun?
questions.why: Pepper is uncountable, so we use a measure word like 'a pinch of'. 'Many pepper' is wrong.

school-c6-english-b.title: Class 6 English · Poorvi (Part B: Units 4–5, Grammar, Writing, Hindi basics & Revision)
school-c6-english-b.description: Class 6 English (Poorvi, NCERT 2024 edition onward) Units 4–5, a full grammar course, writing formats, Hindi grammar basics and revision with mock papers. Original explanations — read the texts themselves in your textbook.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Change of Heart (Unit 4: Sports and Wellness)
courses.summary: A story in the sports and wellness unit about a moment when a character's feelings or decision change. This course teaches character change (before/after), sportsmanship and empathy, conjunctions for reasons and results, and writing a short personal narrative about changing your mind.
outcomes: Learners can trace how a character changes and why
Learners can explain sportsmanship and empathy with examples
Learners can use because, so, although, but to join ideas
Learners can write a personal narrative about a change of heart

scenes.text: Arya is leading the school race and wants the trophy badly.
Behind her, a runner trips and falls.
Arya stops, helps her up, and they finish together.
She doesn't win the trophy, but wins everyone's respect.

steps.title: Character change
steps.body: Many stories show a character who **thinks or feels one way at the start and differently at the end**. Track: What did they want? What happened? What made them change? How do they act now?

steps.title: Sportsmanship
steps.body: Playing fair, respecting rivals, accepting results gracefully, helping others, following rules. Winning matters, but **how** you play matters more.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
In the race scene, what caused Arya's change of heart?

- Seeing a fellow runner fall made her value **kindness** over winning.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Give a real example of sportsmanship.

- Shaking hands with the opponent after losing a match.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Describing only the events, not the reasons for the change.

statements.s: Sportsmanship includes respecting opponents.
A change of heart means changing feelings or decisions.
Good sportspeople never accept defeat.
Helping a fallen rival can show sportsmanship.

quiz.why: 'Change of heart' is an idiom meaning a person changes their feelings or decision. It has nothing to do with surgery or a race.
Sportsmanship means playing fairly and respecting others, win or lose. Boasting and cheating are the opposite.
To see how a character changes, compare how they are at the beginning with how they are at the end. Pages or fonts show nothing about change.
Accepting defeat gracefully shows maturity, because you stay calm and respect the winner. Anger or cheating shows the opposite.
Empathy is understanding how others feel. It is not about winning, speed or ignoring people.

scenes.text: Teacher writes: 'She stopped. Her friend fell.'
Ravi joins: 'She stopped because her friend fell.'
Sara: 'Her friend fell, so she stopped.'
Conjunctions connect cause and effect.

steps.title: Use
steps.body:
- **because** gives a reason: *He rested because he was tired.*
- **so** gives a result: *He was tired, so he rested.*
- **but** shows contrast: *She ran fast but lost.*
- **although** shows unexpected contrast: *Although she lost, she smiled.*
- **and** adds: *She ran and jumped.*

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Join with 'although': She was tired. She finished the race.

- **Although she was tired, she finished the race.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Join with 'so': It rained. The match was postponed.

- **It rained, so the match was postponed.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'Although … but' together ✗ → use only one.

activity.text: He practised daily ___ he wanted to improve. It was late, ___ we went home. ___ she was nervous, she sang beautifully.

quiz.why: 'Because' gives the reason for something. 'So' gives a result, 'but' and 'although' show contrast.
'So' shows the result of something, as in 'It was dark, so we switched on the light.' 'Because' gives the reason instead.

options: Although it rained, but we played.
But although it rained we played.
quiz.why: With 'although' we use only one linking word in a sentence. 'Although it rained, we played' is correct; adding 'but' too is a mistake.
'But' joins two ideas that contrast. 'And' adds, 'because' gives a reason, and 'so' gives a result.
