Falling and still running are in contrast, so 'but' fits: 'He fell but he kept running.' 'Because' or 'so' would change the meaning.

scenes.text: Kabir's team loses the final by one goal.
Coach says, 'It's okay to feel sad. Let's learn from it.'
They write what went well and what to improve.
Next season, they come back stronger.

steps.title: Handling feelings
steps.body:
- Name the feeling (sad, angry, disappointed)
- Breathe slowly; talk to someone you trust
- Look for lessons: what went well, what to practise
- Celebrate effort, not just results

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Healthy response to losing?

- Congratulate the winner, then plan practice.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Unhealthy response?

- Blaming teammates or the referee angrily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Hiding feelings completely — it's healthy to talk about them.

activity.label: Calm-down breathing after a big match

quiz.why: Learning from a loss and planning practice helps you improve. Blaming others, shouting or quitting does not help.
Naming a feeling helps you understand it and become calmer. Hiding it can make it feel bigger.
Effort matters as well as the result, so we should celebrate hard work too. Celebrating only wins ignores those who try hard.

quiz.q: Talking to someone you trust is …
quiz.why: Talking to someone you trust about worries is a healthy and wise thing to do. It is a strength, not a weakness.
Slow, deep breathing helps the body and mind calm down. It does not make you win or run faster.

story.title: The day I changed my mind

scenes.text: Neha didn't want to share her new cricket bat.
She saw her friend practising with a broken stick.
She lent the bat — and they practised together.
She writes about that day for her diary.

steps.title: Personal narrative (100–120 words)
steps.body: First person (I), past tense. Beginning (what you thought/wanted) → event → change → what you learned. Use 2 conjunctions (because, although).

steps.title: Model
steps.body: *I didn't want to lend my new bat because I feared it would get scratched. Although Rohit never asked, I saw him batting with a broken stick. I felt a pinch of guilt, so I handed him my bat. We practised for an hour. That evening, I realised a bat is for playing, and sharing made the game more fun.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Forgetting to show what caused the change.

quiz.why: A personal narrative tells your own story, so it uses first person: I, me, my. Third person is for other people's stories.
A good narrative shows what caused the change, not only the result. That helps the reader understand why it happened.
A diary is about the writer's own day, so it is written in the first person with 'I'. It is not usually third person or passive.
The ending of a narrative shares the lesson learnt, which gives meaning to the story. It should not be a list or blank.

quiz.q: Conjunction for reason in your narrative?
quiz.why: 'Because' gives the reason for something in your story. 'Or', 'then' and 'and' do not show a reason.

questions.q: Sportsmanship means …
questions.why: Sportsmanship means fair play and respect for others. Boasting, cheating and quitting are not sporting.

questions.q: Conjunction of reason?
questions.why: 'Because' introduces a reason. 'But' shows contrast, 'or' gives a choice and 'so' shows a result.

questions.q: 'Change of heart' means …
questions.why: 'Change of heart' is an idiom for changing one's mind or feelings. It is not about the heart as a body part.

questions.q: Join: She was tired. She kept running. (although)
options: Although she was tired, but she kept running.
Although she was tired, she kept running.
questions.why: 'Although' already shows contrast, so we do not add 'but': 'Although she was tired, she kept running.' The other choices are ungrammatical.

questions.q: Empathy is …
questions.why: Empathy is understanding others' feelings and sharing them. It is not speed, strength or winning.

questions.q: A healthy reaction to defeat?
questions.why: Congratulating the winner and practising shows maturity and helps you improve. Blaming, breaking things or quitting does not.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Helping a fallen rival shows sportsmanship. Reason (R): Sportsmanship values respect and kindness over just winning.
questions.why: Both are true: helping a fallen rival shows sportsmanship, which values respect and kindness over winning. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Result conjunction: 'It was dark, ___ we switched on the light.'
questions.why: Switching on the light is the result of the dark, so 'so' fits. 'Because' would give the reason in the wrong place.

questions.q: Read: 'At first Raj sneered at the new boy. By the end of term, he was the first to pick him for his team.' This shows …
questions.why: Raj first sneered, then picked the new boy first for his team, so his feelings changed. That is a change of heart.

questions.q: Which is NOT sportsmanship?
questions.why: Mocking the losing team is disrespectful, so it is not sportsmanship. Following rules, helping and handshakes are sporting.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'Because he was hungry, so he ate.'
options: So he was hungry because he ate.
Because he was hungry, he ate.
questions.why: 'Because' and 'so' both link reason and result, so we use only one: 'Because he was hungry, he ate.' Using both is a mistake.

questions.q: In a personal narrative, the writer's lesson usually appears …
questions.why: The lesson usually comes at the end, where the writer reflects on what happened. It is not placed only in the title or at the start.

questions.q: Best word: 'She lost the match ___ she played her best.'
questions.why: Losing despite playing her best is a contrast, so 'although' fits. 'Because' or 'so' would not make sense.

questions.q: Case: A batsman knows he touched the ball but the umpire says not out. He walks off anyway. This shows …
questions.why: Walking off though the umpire said not out shows honesty and sportsmanship. Cheating would be staying.

questions.q: Which sentence shows cause AND result?
options: He practised daily, so he improved because he was determined.
questions.why: 'He practised daily, so he improved' shows cause and result, and 'because he was determined' adds another reason. The short sentences show neither.

courses.note: Plot details of this text are not retold here — read it in your Poorvi textbook. This course builds the theme, reading, vocabulary, grammar and writing skills around it.

courses.title: Ch 11 · The Winner (poem)
courses.summary: A poem in the sports and wellness unit about what it really means to win. This course builds the theme of perseverance and inner victory, poetic devices (alliteration, contrast), synonyms and antonyms, and writing a motivational message.
outcomes: Learners can explain different meanings of 'winning'
Learners can identify alliteration and contrast in poetry
Learners can use synonyms and antonyms to enrich writing
Learners can write a short motivational message

scenes.text: Meera finishes last in her first swimming race.
But she swam the full length without stopping — her first time ever!
Her coach says, 'You beat yesterday's Meera.'
Winning can mean doing your best and improving.

steps.title: Many kinds of winning
steps.body:
- Coming first in a race
- Beating your own past best (personal best)
- Not giving up (perseverance)
- Playing fairly and helping others
- Learning from failure

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Is someone who finishes 5th but improves their time a winner?

- Yes — in **personal growth**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Which quality helps people win in the long run?

- **Perseverance** (keep trying).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking only the first-place finisher matters.

statements.s: Beating your own record is a kind of winning.
Perseverance means giving up quickly.
Losers can learn valuable lessons.
Cheating to win is real winning.

quiz.why: Perseverance means continuing even when something is difficult. Giving up or cheating is the opposite.
A personal best is your own best performance so far. It is not a team, a medal or a world record.
The poem shows that inner victory comes from effort and growth, not only from trophies. Cheating or luck does not give it.
Failure can be a lesson because it shows what to improve. It is not always shameful or the end.
A true winner plays fair and respects others. Cheating, boasting and blaming others are not winning qualities.

scenes.text: 'Brave boys bounce back' — the class repeats it.
The 'b' sounds make it catchy.
'Not the fastest feet but the firmest heart' — opposites side by side.
Poets use sound and contrast to make ideas memorable.

steps.title: Alliteration
steps.body: Repetition of the same **starting consonant sound** in nearby words: *Sweet silver songs*; *Bold, brave and bright*.

steps.title: Contrast
steps.body: Putting opposite ideas together to make a point: *Lose the race, win the respect.*

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Find alliteration: 'Fast feet fly forward.'

- The repeated **f** sound.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Find contrast: 'He fell down but rose up stronger.'

- **fell down / rose up**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Alliteration depends on sound, not spelling: 'cat' and 'kite' alliterate; 'cat' and 'city' don't.

items.text: Lose the medal, win the friend

quiz.why: Alliteration repeats the same starting consonant sound in nearby words. Rhymes at line ends are different.

quiz.q: 'Lose the race, win the respect' shows …
quiz.why: 'Lose' and 'win' are opposite ideas put together, so this is contrast. It is not a simile or alliteration.
'Cat' and 'kite' both start with the k sound, even though the spellings differ. Alliteration depends on sound, so yes.
Contrast puts opposite ideas together to make a point stand out. Similar words or rhymes do not do that.
'Wild wind whistles' repeats the w sound at the start of each word, which is alliteration. The others do not repeat starting sounds.

scenes.text: Teacher draws a ladder: tiny – small – big – huge.
Students find synonyms for 'brave': bold, fearless, courageous.
And antonyms: cowardly, timid.
A bigger word bank makes writing richer.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Synonyms**: words with similar meanings — win/triumph, try/attempt, brave/courageous
- **Antonyms**: opposite meanings — win/lose, strong/weak, victory/defeat, success/failure

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Synonym of 'persevere'?

- **persist** / keep going

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Antonym of 'victory'?

- **defeat**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Synonyms aren't always perfect swaps: 'house' and 'home' differ in feeling.

activity.prompt: Match each word to its antonym.

quiz.why: 'Courageous' has nearly the same meaning as 'brave'. 'Scared', 'timid' and 'weak' mean the opposite or something else.
The opposite of 'win' is 'lose'. Triumph, succeed and gain are close to 'win' in meaning.
'Try' means the same as 'attempt'. 'End', 'fail' and 'quit' do not.
The opposite of 'success' is 'failure'. Win, victory and gain are similar to success.
'Victory' means the same as 'triumph'. Fall, defeat and loss mean the opposite.

scenes.text: Before sports day, Class 6 writes notes for each runner.
'Run your race, not theirs!'
Runners stick the notes on their bags.
Everyone runs with a smile.

steps.title: Format (40–60 words)
steps.body: Address the person → encourage effort → mention a strength → end with a short, memorable line (use alliteration or contrast).

steps.title: Model
steps.body: *Dear Riya, you've trained every morning this month. Remember your strong start and steady breathing. Whatever the clock says, you've already won by not giving up. Run your race — bold, brave and bright! — Your friend, Isha*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Pressuring ('You MUST win') instead of encouraging effort.

items: I praised effort, not only results

quiz.why: A motivational message should encourage effort so the reader feels able to try. Pressure, blame or mocking would discourage them.

options: Run your race — bold and brave!
quiz.why: 'Run your race — bold and brave!' is positive and memorable. The other lines are negative or pressure the reader.
Mentioning a real strength makes the message sincere and specific. Random facts or prices do not.
A short message is about 40–60 words, enough to encourage without being long. 500 words or a page is too long, and one word is too little.
Effort praise says what the person did, like training hard every day. Saying they are lucky or slow, or that they must win, does not praise effort.

questions.q: Synonym of 'victory'?
questions.why: 'Triumph' is a synonym of 'victory'. Failure, defeat and loss are opposites.

questions.q: Antonym of 'strong'?
questions.why: The opposite of 'strong' is 'weak'. Mighty, powerful and tough are synonyms.

questions.q: Perseverance means …
questions.why: Perseverance means not giving up even when things are hard. Resting or giving up is not perseverance.

questions.q: 'Big brave bears' is an example of …
questions.why: 'Big brave bears' repeats the b sound at the start of words, which is alliteration. There is no comparison, so it is not a simile or metaphor.

questions.q: 'Lose the race, win the respect' shows …
questions.why: 'Lose' and 'win' are opposite ideas put side by side, which is contrast. There is no repeated sound or rhyme.

questions.q: A personal best is …
questions.why: A personal best is the best performance you have achieved so far. It is not a coach or a team trophy.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Someone who finishes last can be a winner. Reason (R): Winning can mean improving and not giving up.
questions.why: Both are true: finishing last can still be winning if you improved and did not give up. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Antonym of 'begin'?
questions.why: The opposite of 'begin' is 'finish'. Open, launch and start are similar to 'begin'.

questions.q: Which is alliteration?
questions.why: 'Tiny turtles trot' repeats the t sound at the start of the words, so it is alliteration. The others lack repeated starting sounds.

questions.q: Read: 'She did not win the gold, but she won her fear.' Main idea?
questions.why: The line says she did not win the gold but overcame her fear, so overcoming fear is her victory. It is not about being afraid of gold.

questions.q: Best synonym for 'persist' in: 'He persisted until he solved the puzzle.'
questions.why: 'Persisted until he solved the puzzle' means he kept trying. Giving up would not lead to solving it.

questions.q: Which is the most encouraging message?
options: You've trained so well — enjoy the race!
questions.why: 'You've trained so well — enjoy the race!' is positive and supportive. The other messages add pressure or fear.

questions.q: Which shows contrast?
options: Fall seven times, stand up eight.
questions.why: 'Fall seven times, stand up eight' puts falling against standing up, which is contrast. The others have no opposing ideas.

questions.q: Case: A student fails a test, studies harder and passes the next one. Which word fits him?
questions.why: A student who fails, studies harder and passes shows perseverance, meaning not giving up. Boastful, cowardly or careless does not fit.

questions.q: Which pair are NOT antonyms?
questions.why: 'Win' and 'triumph' mean nearly the same, so they are synonyms. The other pairs are opposites.

courses.note: Plot details of this text are not retold here — read it in your Poorvi textbook. This course builds the theme, reading, vocabulary, grammar and writing skills around it.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Yoga — A Way of Life
courses.summary: An informational text about yoga as a practice for body and mind: what yoga means, asanas and pranayama, benefits, safety, and International Day of Yoga (21 June). Reading for main idea and details, the present simple for habits and facts, and writing a short informative paragraph.
outcomes: Learners can explain what yoga is and its benefits for body and mind
Learners can follow safe practice guidelines for simple asanas and breathing
Learners can use the present simple for facts and routines
Learners can write an informative paragraph with a main idea and details

scenes.text: Every morning, Anvi and her grandfather unroll mats on the terrace.
They stretch, balance and breathe slowly.
Anvi feels calm and focused before school.
Millions around the world do yoga on 21 June.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: **Yoga** comes from the Sanskrit root *yuj* — to join or unite — often explained as uniting body, breath and mind. It includes **asanas** (postures), **pranayama** (breathing practices), **relaxation** and **meditation**, along with values like discipline and non-violence.

steps.title: International Day of Yoga
steps.body: The United Nations declared **21 June** as International Day of Yoga in **December 2014**, after India proposed it; it was first celebrated in **2015**. 21 June is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

steps.title: Benefits
steps.body: Flexibility, strength, balance, better posture, calmer mind, better focus and sleep. It's a lifelong habit — 'a way of life'.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Main idea of a paragraph that says yoga improves flexibility, calm and focus.

- **Yoga benefits both body and mind.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Why 21 June?

- It's the **longest day** in the Northern Hemisphere; the proposal was adopted by the UN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking yoga is only stretching — breathing and calm attention are central.

activity.text: International Day of Yoga is on ___ June. Asanas are yoga ___. Pranayama is about ___.

quiz.why: The word 'yoga' comes from the root 'yuj', which means to join or unite, such as body and mind. It has nothing to do with eating or running.
Asanas are yoga postures, the body positions held during practice. They are not foods, songs or games.
Pranayama is the yoga practice of controlling the breath. It is not about singing, jumping or eating.
International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June each year. The other dates belong to different days.
It was first celebrated in 2015, after the UN declared it in December 2014. The other years do not match.

scenes.text: Kunal tries Vrikshasana (tree pose) and wobbles.
His teacher says, 'Fix your eyes on one point.'
He steadies and holds for 20 seconds.
Balance improves with practice, not force.

steps.title: A few beginner asanas
steps.body:
- **Tadasana** (mountain pose): stand tall, feet together, arms up — posture
- **Vrikshasana** (tree pose): stand on one leg, other foot on inner thigh/calf (not the knee), palms together — balance
- **Bhujangasana** (cobra pose): lie on stomach, lift chest gently — back strength
- **Balasana** (child's pose): kneel, fold forward — rest
- **Shavasana** (corpse pose): lie flat, relax — calm

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Practise on an empty or light stomach, on a mat, slowly and without pain; never force a stretch; breathe normally; stop if you feel dizzy; learn from a trained teacher; people with health conditions should ask a doctor first.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which pose helps balance?

- **Vrikshasana**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Where should the foot rest in tree pose?

- On the **inner thigh or calf**, not on the knee joint.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Competing to stretch the farthest — yoga is not a contest.

activity.prompt: Match the asana to its main benefit.

quiz.why: Vrikshasana is the tree pose, since 'vriksha' means tree. Tadasana is mountain pose, Shavasana is relaxation and Balasana is child's pose.
Yoga should be done slowly and without pain, because forcing the body can cause injury. It is not a race, and a heavy meal beforehand is not advised.
If you feel dizzy, stop and rest so you stay safe. Jumping or continuing faster could make it worse.
Shavasana is a resting pose done lying down for relaxation. It is not for running, jumping or balancing.
Yoga is not a competition, because each person works at their own pace. It is for people of all ages, not only athletes or adults.

lessons.title: Present simple for facts and habits

scenes.text: 'Grandpa wakes at five. He drinks warm water. He does yoga for thirty minutes.'
Anvi writes his routine for a class project.
She notices 'wakes, drinks, does' — all end in -s.
Present simple describes habits.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: For **habits/routines** (I practise yoga daily), **facts** (Yoga improves flexibility), **timetables**.

steps.title: Form
steps.body:
- I/you/we/they + base verb: *They stretch.*
- He/she/it + verb **-s/-es**: *She stretches. He does. It goes.*
- Negative: do/does not + base: *He does not skip.*
- Question: Do/Does + subject + base? *Does she practise?*
- Time words: always, usually, often, every day

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'She practise yoga every day.'

- **She practises yoga every day.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Make a question: 'He meditates in the morning.'

- **Does he meditate in the morning?**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'Does she practises?' ✗ → 'Does she practise?' ✓

activity.text: My mother (do) ___ yoga daily. The sun (rise) ___ in the east. We (not / eat) ___ before yoga.

quiz.why: With he/she/it in present simple, verbs ending in -ch take -es: 'stretches'. 'Stretchs' is a wrong spelling.
After 'does' we use the base verb, so 'Does she breathe slowly?' is correct. 'Breathes' with 'does' is a mistake.
Present simple is used for habits and general facts, like 'She practises daily'. It is not mainly for the past or the future.
With 'they' the negative is 'do not' plus the base verb: 'They do not practise.' 'Does' is for he/she/it.
For he/she/it, 'go' becomes 'goes' by adding -es. 'Goed' and 'gos' are not words.

scenes.text: Anvi wants to invite classmates to a new yoga club.
She writes a paragraph explaining yoga's benefits.
Main idea first, then three details, then a closing line.
Twenty students join!

steps.title: Structure (80–100 words)
steps.body: Topic sentence (main idea) → 3 supporting facts → concluding sentence. Use present simple and linking words (also, moreover, finally).

steps.title: Model
steps.body: *Yoga is a simple way to keep the body and mind healthy. It improves flexibility and posture. It also builds balance and strength through poses like Vrikshasana. Moreover, slow breathing in pranayama calms the mind and helps us focus in class. Just fifteen minutes a day can make a difference, so let's start together at the yoga club!*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing opinions without facts in an informative paragraph.

quiz.why: Informative writing mainly gives facts and explains a topic. It is not a poem or a joke.

quiz.q: Linking word to add a point?
quiz.why: 'Moreover' adds another point to what was said. 'Although' and 'but' show contrast and 'because' gives a reason.
A topic sentence states the main idea and usually comes first in a paragraph. This helps the reader know what follows.
Facts and general truths are written in present simple. Future or past perfect would not fit.
A good closing sentence sums up the main idea or invites the reader to act. Adding a new topic would confuse the reader.

questions.q: Yoga's root 'yuj' means …
questions.why: The root 'yuj' means to unite or join, which is where 'yoga' comes from. It does not mean to run, eat or fight.

questions.q: International Day of Yoga?
questions.why: International Day of Yoga is on 21 June. The other dates are different occasions.

questions.q: Asana means …
questions.why: 'Asana' means posture, a position of the body in yoga. Breath is 'prana', so the other meanings are wrong.

questions.q: Correct:
options: She practised daily every day now.
questions.why: With 'she' in present simple, the verb takes -es: 'practises'. 'Practise' and 'practising' are wrong here, and 'practised... now' mixes tenses.

questions.q: Pranayama is about …
questions.why: Pranayama is the practice of breath control. It is not sleeping, eating or running.

questions.q: Tree pose helps …
questions.why: Standing on one leg in tree pose trains balance. It is not mainly for eyesight, hearing or digestion.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Yoga should never be forced. Reason (R): Forcing stretches can cause injury.
questions.why: Both are true: yoga should not be forced because forcing stretches can cause injury. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: UN declared International Day of Yoga in …
questions.why: The UN declared the day in December 2014, and the first celebration was in 2015. So the declaration year is 2014.

questions.q: Question form: 'He meditates.'
questions.why: In a question with 'does' the verb goes back to base form: 'Does he meditate?' The -s moves to 'does'.

questions.q: Which is NOT safe practice?
options: Doing poses right after a heavy meal
questions.why: Doing poses right after a heavy meal is unsafe, as it can cause discomfort. Stopping if dizzy, breathing normally and using a mat are safe.

questions.q: Read: 'Ten minutes of slow breathing before exams helped Riya feel calm.' Main idea?
questions.why: Slow breathing helped Riya feel calm before exams, so the idea is that breathing practice can reduce stress. The passage does not say exams are easy.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'Does yoga improves focus?'
questions.why: After 'does' the main verb takes the base form, so 'Does yoga improve focus?' is right. 'Improves' is a mistake.

questions.q: Why is 21 June chosen?
options: It is the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere
questions.why: 21 June is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere (the summer solstice). It was chosen for this reason, not randomly.

questions.q: Case: A friend with a back injury wants to try cobra pose. Best advice?
options: Ask a doctor and a trained teacher first
questions.why: A person with a back injury should ask a doctor and a trained teacher first, because some poses could make it worse. Ignoring pain is unsafe.

questions.q: Which linking word best fits: 'Yoga builds strength. ___, it calms the mind.'
questions.why: 'Moreover' adds another point: yoga builds strength, and also calms the mind. 'But' and 'although' show contrast, and 'because' gives a reason.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Hamara Bharat — Incredible India! (Unit 5: Culture and Tradition)
courses.summary: A text celebrating India's variety — landscapes, monuments, crafts, foods, festivals and languages. Reading descriptive and persuasive writing, proper nouns and capital letters, adjectives of quality, and writing a travel brochure.
outcomes: Learners can describe India's diversity with examples from different regions
Learners can identify persuasive language in tourism writing
Learners can use capital letters for proper nouns correctly
Learners can write a short travel brochure

scenes.text: Class 6 plans a dream trip around India on a big map.
Snow in Ladakh, backwaters in Kerala, deserts in Rajasthan.
The Taj Mahal, Konark, Hampi, the Red Fort.
'So much in one country!' says Neel.

steps.title: Diversity examples
steps.body:
- Landscapes: Himalayas, Thar Desert, Western Ghats, Sundarbans mangroves, Kerala backwaters, island chains
- Monuments and heritage sites: Taj Mahal (Agra), Sun Temple (Konark), Hampi (Karnataka), Ajanta–Ellora caves, Qutub Minar, Rani ki Vav (Patan)
- Crafts: Madhubani painting, Pattachitra, Chikankari, Bidriware, Blue Pottery
- Classical dances: Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Odissi, Kuchipudi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam, Sattriya

steps.title: Incredible India
steps.body: 'Incredible India' is the name of India's official tourism campaign, inviting visitors to explore its variety.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Name two heritage sites in different states.

- **Konark** (Odisha), **Hampi** (Karnataka).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Match a dance to its state: Kathakali → **Kerala**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Calling the Taj Mahal a temple or placing it in Delhi — it's a mausoleum in Agra.

activity.prompt: Match the place or art to its state.

quiz.why: The Taj Mahal is in Agra, Uttar Pradesh. Jaipur, Delhi and Lucknow have other monuments.
Kathakali is a classical dance-drama from Kerala. It is not from Punjab, Gujarat or Assam.
Madhubani is a style of painting from Bihar. It is not a food, dance or river.
'Incredible India' is the tourism campaign that promotes India to visitors. It is not a river, monument or law.
Kerala is famous for its backwaters, a network of lagoons and canals. Punjab, Rajasthan and Ladakh are known for other things.

scenes.text: Neel reads a tourism advert: 'Glide through emerald backwaters…'
The words make him want to go!
Teacher points out vivid adjectives and direct appeals.
Persuasive writing makes readers act.

steps.title: Descriptive language
steps.body: Vivid adjectives and sense details: *emerald backwaters, golden dunes, misty hills, aromatic spices*.

steps.title: Persuasive techniques
steps.body:
- Direct address: *you, your*
- Imperatives: *Come, Discover, Experience*
- Superlatives: *the finest, the most colourful*
- Rhetorical questions: *Why wait?*
- Facts and numbers to build trust

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Make persuasive: 'Rajasthan has deserts.'

- *Ride a camel across Rajasthan's golden dunes under a sky full of stars — why wait?*

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Spot the technique: 'Experience the magic of Hampi!'

- **Imperative** + vivid noun 'magic'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Exaggerating falsely — persuasive writing should still be honest.

quiz.why: Imperatives are commands like 'Visit!' or 'Explore!', and ads use them to urge readers to act. They do not describe the past.
'Emerald' is a vivid adjective that paints a picture of the deep green water. It is not a verb or number.
A rhetorical question is asked for effect and does not expect an answer. It makes the reader think.
Persuasive writing should be honest, because false claims mislead readers and lose trust. Being boring or silent would not persuade.
Direct address speaks to the reader as 'you'. 'They', 'it' and 'one' talk about someone else.

scenes.text: A brochure reads: 'visit the taj mahal in agra in october.'
Asha circles every word that needs a capital.
Names of places, monuments, months and the first word.
'Visit the Taj Mahal in Agra in October.'

steps.title: Use capitals for
steps.body:
- First word of a sentence
- **Proper nouns**: names of people, places, rivers, mountains, monuments, festivals, days, months, languages (Ganga, Himalayas, Diwali, Monday, March, Tamil)
- The pronoun **I**
- Titles of books/films (main words)

Not for seasons in general (summer, winter) or common nouns (river, city).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'we visited the red fort on independence day.'

- **We visited the Red Fort on Independence Day.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Common or proper: city / Mumbai

- city: common; **Mumbai**: proper.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Capitalising common nouns randomly (the River) ✗ unless part of a name.

quiz.why: 'Ganga' is the name of a particular river, so it is a proper noun and needs a capital letter. 'Water', 'boat' and 'river' are common nouns.
'I' and names of places like Pune are always capitalised. Only the first sentence is fully correct.
Seasons like winter are common nouns, so they usually do not take capitals. Names of people and places do.
Names of languages, such as Tamil, are proper nouns and always need capitals. They are not verbs.
'Qutub Minar' is the name of a monument, so both words begin with capitals. The other sentences are missing capitals or have extra ones.

scenes.text: Each group makes a brochure for their home state.
They add places to visit, food to try, festivals to enjoy.
A catchy title and a call to action.
The best brochure goes on the school notice board.

steps.title: Brochure format
steps.body:
- Catchy title and slogan
- Short sections with headings: Places to see / Taste / Celebrate / How to reach
- Vivid adjectives, imperatives, true facts
- Call to action and contact/website (made up for practice)

steps.title: Model section
steps.body:
**Discover Odisha — the Soul of Incredible India!**
*See:* the stone chariot of Konark's Sun Temple.
*Taste:* chhena poda, a baked cottage-cheese sweet.
*Celebrate:* Rath Yatra in Puri.
Come, experience Odisha's golden beaches and timeless temples!

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing long paragraphs; brochures need short, scannable text.

quiz.why: Brochure text should be short and scannable so readers can pick up the main points quickly. Very long text or tiny print is hard to read.
A call to action tells the reader what to do next. 'Book your trip today!' does that.
Facts in brochures must be true, because false claims mislead people. Exaggerating or inventing is dishonest.
Headings help readers find the information they want fast. They do not confuse or make readers skip everything.
Rath Yatra is famous in Puri, Odisha, with the huge chariots of Lord Jagannath. It is not celebrated this way in Kochi, Shimla or Jaipur.

questions.q: Taj Mahal is in …
questions.why: The Taj Mahal is in Agra. It is not in Mumbai, Delhi or Hyderabad.

questions.q: Which is a proper noun?
questions.why: 'Kerala' is the name of a specific state, so it is a proper noun. 'State', 'river' and 'beach' are common nouns.

questions.q: Kathak is a …
questions.why: Kathak is a classical dance of India. It is not a monument, food or painting.

questions.q: Correct:
questions.why: Names of places and months need capitals, so 'Hampi' and 'May' begin with capital letters. The first word of a sentence does too.

questions.q: 'Discover the magic!' is …
questions.why: 'Discover the magic!' is a command that urges readers to act and attracts them, so it is persuasive. It is not a fact or a question.

questions.q: Konark Sun Temple is in …
questions.why: The Konark Sun Temple is in Odisha. It is not in Gujarat, Bihar or Tamil Nadu.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Tourism ads use imperatives. Reason (R): Imperatives urge readers to take action.
questions.why: Both are true: tourism ads use imperatives because commands urge readers to take action. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is a rhetorical question?
questions.why: 'Why wait any longer?' is asked for effect and expects no answer. The others need real answers.

questions.q: Madhubani art is from …
questions.why: Madhubani art is from Bihar. It is not from Kerala, Punjab or Goa.

questions.q: Which is a descriptive phrase?
questions.why: 'Misty blue mountains' describes how the mountains look. 'Book now' and 'call us' are commands.

questions.q: Correct the capitals: 'my uncle lives near the river yamuna in delhi.'
options: My Uncle Lives Near The River Yamuna In Delhi.
My uncle lives near the river Yamuna in Delhi.
my uncle lives near the River yamuna in Delhi.
questions.why: 'Uncle' is not a name here, so it stays small, but 'Yamuna' and 'Delhi' are names and take capitals. 'River' stays small as a common noun.

questions.q: Best brochure slogan?
options: Rajasthan — where every fort tells a story!
questions.why: 'Rajasthan — where every fort tells a story!' is catchy and creates interest. The others are plain and dull.

questions.q: Which is NOT a classical dance of India?
questions.why: Ballet is a Western dance form. Bharatanatyam, Odissi and Kuchipudi are Indian classical dances.

questions.q: Case: A brochure says 'Our beach is the cleanest in the universe!' Problem?
questions.why: 'Cleanest in the universe' cannot be true, so it is an untrue exaggeration. Brochures must be honest.

questions.q: Which sentence uses both a vivid adjective and an imperative?
options: Explore the emerald backwaters of Kerala!
questions.why: 'Explore the emerald backwaters of Kerala!' has the command 'Explore' and the vivid adjective 'emerald'. The others have neither or only one.

courses.title: Ch 14 · The Kites (poem)
courses.summary: A poem in the culture and tradition unit about kites — their colours, flight and the joy of kite-flying festivals. This course teaches imagery of movement and colour, onomatopoeia, action verbs and adverbs, and writing a short descriptive poem.
outcomes: Learners can identify imagery of colour and movement in a poem
Learners can explain onomatopoeia and find examples
Learners can use action verbs and adverbs vividly
Learners can write a short poem describing a festival scene

scenes.text: On Makar Sankranti in Ahmedabad, every rooftop is full of families.
Red, yellow, green kites dance in the sky.
'Kai po che!' someone shouts as a kite is cut.
The sky looks like a moving painting.

steps.title: Kite festivals
steps.body: Kite flying is a joyful tradition in many parts of India — especially **Uttarayan/Makar Sankranti** (Gujarat, January), and on **Independence Day** in Delhi and other cities, and **Basant Panchami** in parts of north India. It brings families and neighbours together.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Use cotton thread, never glass-coated 'manja' (it injures birds and people and is banned in many places); stay away from electric wires; fly on safe rooftops with railings and adult supervision.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Why is glass-coated manja dangerous?

- It can **cut birds and people**, including motorcyclists.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Name a festival linked with kite flying.

- **Uttarayan / Makar Sankranti**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Flying kites near power lines or on roofs without railings.

items: Rooftop with railings and an adult present
Never chase a kite onto a road
Rescue tangled birds only with an adult's/animal helpline's help

quiz.why: Uttarayan, the kite festival, is celebrated in Gujarat. It is not mainly celebrated in Goa, Assam or Kerala.
Glass-coated manja can cut birds and people badly, so it is dangerous. Its colour or price is not the problem.
Fly kites away from electric wires, because the string can cause shocks. Parks and open fields are safe.
Kite festivals bring people together to share fun and joy. They are community events.
Makar Sankranti falls in January, when kites are flown. It does not fall in October, July or December.

lessons.title: Imagery of colour and movement · Onomatopoeia

scenes.text: 'The kites swoop, soar and swirl.'
'Scarlet and saffron specks against the blue.'
'The string goes whirr! The paper flutters, flap-flap.'
Poems can make us see and hear a scene.

steps.title: Imagery
steps.body: Words appealing to sight (scarlet, saffron, specks), motion (swoop, soar, dip, dart, tug), sound and touch.

steps.title: Onomatopoeia
steps.body: Words that imitate sounds: whirr, whoosh, flap, buzz, swish, rustle, crack.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Find onomatopoeia: 'The wind whooshed and the kite went flap.'

- **whooshed**, **flap**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Make a movement image for a falling kite.

- *It tumbled, twirled and drifted down like a dry leaf.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Using flat verbs ('the kite went up') when vivid ones exist (soared, climbed).

quiz.why: Onomatopoeia is when a word imitates a sound, like 'buzz'. Names, colours and numbers are not sounds.
'Buzz' sounds like the noise it names, so it is onomatopoeia. 'High', 'blue' and 'kite' do not.
'Soared' shows vivid movement, rising high in the air. 'Had', 'was' and 'went' are plain.
'Scarlet specks' describes colour and shape, which we see. So it appeals to sight.
'Whoosh' imitates the sound of air rushing past. It does not describe a colour or silence.

scenes.text: 'The kite flew.' Teacher asks, 'How?'
'The kite flew swiftly / gracefully / wildly.'
These -ly words are adverbs.
Adverbs tell how, when, where.

steps.title: Adverbs
steps.body: Words that describe verbs: **how** (gracefully, quickly), **when** (now, soon, yesterday), **where** (up, everywhere, outside). Many are adjective + **-ly**: swift → swiftly; gentle → gently; happy → happily.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Add an adverb: 'The children shouted.'

- *The children shouted **joyfully**.*

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Form adverbs: easy, careful, gentle.

- **easily, carefully, gently**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'He runs quick' ✗ → 'He runs quickly' ✓
- 'good' is an adjective; the adverb is 'well'.

activity.text: The kite rose (graceful) ___. Hold the string (careful) ___. She flies kites very (good) ___.

quiz.why: Adjectives ending in -y change y to i and add -ly: happy becomes 'happily'. 'Happyly' is wrongly spelt.
Adverbs mainly describe verbs (how, when or where something is done). They can also describe adjectives or other adverbs.
'Well' is the adverb telling how she sings. 'Good' is an adjective, and 'goodly' is not correct.
'Outside' tells where something happens, so it is an adverb of place. 'Softly' and 'quickly' tell how, 'yesterday' tells when.
For adjectives ending in -le, drop the e and add -y: gentle becomes 'gently'. 'Gentlely' is wrongly spelt.

scenes.text: Riya writes 6 lines about Uttarayan.
She uses two colours, two movement verbs and a sound word.
She recites it in class.
Applause!

steps.title: Recipe (6–8 lines)
steps.body: Set the scene (time, place) → colours → movement verbs + adverbs → a sound word → a feeling at the end. Rhyme is optional.

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
*Morning sun on rooftop walls,*
*Saffron kites and scarlet sails,*
*They swoop and soar, they dip and climb,*
*The strings go whirr, one at a time.*
*A cheer goes up — a kite set free!*
*The whole bright sky belongs to me.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Listing nouns only; add verbs, adverbs and feelings.

items: A feeling in the last line

quiz.why: A festival poem should include sense details of what we see, hear, smell and feel. Maps or recipes do not suit it.
The ending line should share a feeling so the reader is left with it. An empty or random line would not.
Rhyme is optional, since a poem can be good without it. It is neither compulsory nor banned.
'Climb' is an action verb showing movement. 'Blue' and 'sky' are not verbs, and 'whirr' is a sound word.
'Whirr' imitates a sound, so it is onomatopoeia. 'Morning', 'saffron' and 'rooftop' do not imitate sounds.

questions.q: Onomatopoeia?
questions.why: 'Buzz' imitates the sound of a bee, so it is onomatopoeia. 'Tall', 'bright' and 'kite' do not.

questions.q: Adverb in 'The kite rose quickly.'
questions.why: 'Quickly' tells how the kite rose, so it is the adverb. 'Rose' is the verb and 'kite' the noun.

questions.q: Uttarayan is mainly celebrated in …
questions.why: Uttarayan is mainly celebrated in Gujarat with kite flying. It is not mainly in Kerala, Punjab or Assam.

questions.q: Adverb of 'careful'?
questions.why: Adjective 'careful' becomes an adverb by adding -ly: 'carefully'. Other spellings are wrong.

questions.q: Why avoid glass manja?
questions.why: Glass manja is sharp and injures birds and people. Its colour or weight is not the reason to avoid it.

questions.q: A movement image?
questions.why: 'The kite darted and dipped' shows motion with action verbs. The other lines only state facts.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Poets use onomatopoeia. Reason (R): It helps readers hear the scene.
questions.why: Both are true: poets use onomatopoeia so that readers can hear the scene. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Correct: 'He flies kites very good.'
questions.why: 'Good' is an adjective, so we need the adverb 'well' to describe how he flies. 'Goodly' is not a word, and the sentence is not correct as it is.

questions.q: 'Scarlet and saffron' appeal to …
questions.why: Scarlet and saffron are colours, which we see. So they appeal to sight.

questions.q: Which is an adverb of time?
questions.why: 'Yesterday' tells when something happened, so it is an adverb of time. 'Slowly' is manner and 'here' and 'outside' are place.

questions.q: Read: 'The kites hung like bright stars stitched on a blue cloth.' Device?
questions.why: The kites are compared to bright stars with the word 'like', so it is a simile. It does not imitate a sound.

questions.q: Choose the most vivid sentence.
options: The scarlet kite swooped gracefully over the rooftops.
questions.why: 'The scarlet kite swooped gracefully over the rooftops' has a colour adjective, a strong verb and an adverb. The others are plain.

questions.q: Safe place to fly kites?
options: An open field away from wires
questions.why: An open field away from wires is safest, since there is no risk from power lines, roads or edges. The other places are dangerous.

questions.q: Which line has onomatopoeia AND an adverb?
options: The string whirred noisily in the wind.
questions.why: 'Whirred' is a sound word and 'noisily' is an adverb, so the line has both. The others lack one of them.

questions.q: Case: A tangled bird is stuck in kite string on a tree. Best action?
options: Inform an adult or an animal helpline
questions.why: Do not climb or pull alone, since it is risky and may hurt the bird. An adult or an animal helpline can help safely.

courses.note: Plot details of this text are not retold here — read it in your Poorvi textbook. This course builds the theme, reading, vocabulary, grammar and writing skills around it.

courses.title: Ch 15 · Ila Sachani: Embroidering Dreams with her Feet
courses.summary: A true-life text about Ila Sachani from Gujarat, who could not use her hands for needlework and learned to embroider with her feet, creating beautiful traditional embroidery. This course explores determination and ability, India's embroidery traditions, words for qualities, the present perfect for achievements, and writing a profile of an inspiring person.
outcomes: Learners can describe how determination helped Ila Sachani pursue her art
Learners can name some Indian embroidery traditions
Learners can use the present perfect to describe achievements
Learners can write a respectful profile of an inspiring person

scenes.text: As a girl in Gujarat, Ila watches the women in her family embroider.
Her hands can't hold a needle, so she tries with her feet.
It takes years of patient practice.
Her embroidery becomes admired for its fine detail.

steps.title: The main idea (in our words)
steps.body: Ila Sachani faced a physical challenge that stopped her from using her hands for needlework. Instead of giving up, she trained herself to **embroider with her feet**, and her work became known for its skill and beauty. Her story shows **determination, patience and creativity**, and that disability does not define what a person can achieve. (Read the full text in your textbook for details.)

steps.title: Respectful language
steps.body: Say *a person with a disability*, focus on abilities and achievements, avoid pity or labels. Everyone deserves dignity.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which quality helped her most?

- **Determination** (also patience, practice).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What can we learn?

- Find another way when one door closes; practise patiently.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Describing people with disabilities only through what they can't do.

statements.s: Ila Sachani embroiders using her feet.
Determination helped her develop her skill.
Respectful language focuses on pity.
Her skill came from years of practice.

quiz.why: Ila Sachani is from Gujarat. The other states are not her home.
Ila Sachani was born without arms, so she does her embroidery with her feet. She does not use her hands, mouth or only a machine.
Her story shows determination: she kept practising until she could embroider with her feet. Greed, laziness and anger are not shown.
'A person with a disability' puts the person first and shows respect. Words like 'cripple', 'poor thing' or 'helpless' insult or pity people.

options: there can be another way to reach a dream
quiz.why: Ila's story teaches that when one way is closed, another way can still lead to a dream. Giving up early or calling dreams impossible is the opposite of her example.

scenes.text: At a crafts fair, Nidhi sees embroidery from many states.
Shiny mirror-work from Kutch, white-on-white Chikankari from Lucknow.
Phulkari from Punjab, Kantha from Bengal.
Each stitch tells a regional story.

steps.title: Some traditions
steps.body:
- **Kutch / mirror-work** (Gujarat): colourful threads with small mirrors
- **Chikankari** (Lucknow, UP): delicate white thread on light cloth
- **Phulkari** (Punjab): bright 'flower-work'
- **Kantha** (West Bengal, Odisha): running stitch on layered cloth
- **Kasuti** (Karnataka), **Zardozi** (metallic thread work)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which embroidery uses small mirrors?

- **Kutch mirror-work** (Gujarat).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Phulkari means …

- **flower-work** (Punjab).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing up embroidery (stitching on cloth) with weaving (making cloth on a loom).

activity.prompt: Match the embroidery to its region.

quiz.why: Chikankari, a delicate white-on-white embroidery, comes from Lucknow. Kutch, Amritsar and Mysuru are known for other crafts.
Phulkari means 'flower work', since 'phul' is flower and 'kari' is work. It is a Punjabi embroidery with flower patterns.
Embroidery is decorative stitching on cloth that already exists. Weaving makes the cloth on a loom, and dyeing and printing add colour.
Kantha, from Bengal, is made with simple running stitches. It does not use glue or only gold or mirrors.
Mirror-work embroidery is famous in Kutch, Gujarat, where tiny mirrors are stitched into cloth. Assam, Kerala and Bihar are better known for other crafts.

scenes.text: Asha writes about her aunt, a craftswoman.
'She has trained 50 women. She has won awards. She has shown her work in Delhi.'
'has + past participle' — the present perfect.
It shows achievements up to now.

steps.title: Form and use
steps.body:
**has/have + past participle**: She **has embroidered** many saris. They **have visited** fairs.

Use it for achievements/experiences up to now, without a specific past time. With a specific time, use simple past: *She **won** an award in 2019.*

steps.title: Past participles
steps.body: work → worked; train → trained; win → won; show → shown; make → made; teach → taught; see → seen

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'She has win many hearts.'

- **She has won many hearts.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Choose: 'She (has shown / showed) her work in 2022.'

- **showed** (specific time).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'She has went' ✗ → 'She has gone' ✓

activity.text: She (teach) has ___ many students. They (make) have ___ beautiful shawls. I (see) have ___ her work.

quiz.why: Present perfect is made with has/have plus the past participle, like 'has finished'. 'Will + verb' is future and 'was + -ing' is past continuous.
The past participle of 'win' is 'won', and with 'she' we use 'has'. 'Winned' is not a word and 'she have' is wrong.
'In 2019' names a finished time in the past, so we use simple past. Present perfect is not used with a fixed past time.
The past participle of 'go' is 'gone', as in 'has gone'. 'Went' is the simple past, and 'goed' is not a word.
'They' is plural, so present perfect takes 'have': 'They have visited Kutch.' 'Is' and 'has' are for singular subjects.

lessons.title: Write a profile of an inspiring person

scenes.text: Kabir chooses his neighbour, a tailor who taught himself after an accident.
He interviews him with five questions.
He writes a profile: who, challenge, effort, achievement, lesson.
The profile is pinned on the school wall.

steps.title: Profile structure (120 words)
steps.body: Introduction (who, where) → challenge → how they worked at it → achievements (present perfect) → what we can learn. Use respectful language.

steps.title: Model opening
steps.body: *Mrs. Kamala Devi has stitched school uniforms in our town for thirty years. After losing the use of two fingers in an accident, she…*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Making up facts about a real person — ask them or check sources.

quiz.why: A profile describes a real person: who they are and what they have done. It is not about a recipe or a machine.

quiz.q: Facts in a profile must be …
quiz.why: Facts in a profile must be checked and true, because a profile is about a real person. Exaggerating or inventing facts is dishonest.

quiz.q: Tense for achievements up to now?
quiz.why: Present perfect links the past to now, so it suits achievements up to now, like 'She has won many awards'. Future or past continuous does not fit.
Respectful writing focuses on a person's abilities and effort, not on labels or pity. Jokes would be unkind.
A good final paragraph shares the lesson or takeaway for the reader. A recipe or a new person would take the reader away from the point.

questions.q: Ila Sachani embroiders with her …
questions.why: Ila Sachani embroiders with her feet, because she was born without arms. The story is about doing art in her own way.

questions.q: Chikankari is from …
questions.why: Chikankari is a delicate embroidery from Lucknow. Kutch is known for mirror work, so it does not fit here.

questions.q: Present perfect: 'She ___ finished.'
questions.why: 'She' is singular, so present perfect uses 'has': 'She has finished.' 'Have' is for I/you/we/they.

questions.q: Phulkari is from …
questions.why: Phulkari, meaning 'flower work', is the embroidery of Punjab. Odisha, Bengal and Karnataka are known for other crafts.

questions.q: Past participle of 'teach'?
questions.why: 'Teach' is irregular: its past participle is 'taught'. 'Teached' and 'taughted' are not words.

questions.q: Main lesson of Ila's story?
questions.why: Ila's story shows that determination finds a way, even without hands. Giving up and saying art is easy do not match it.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Respectful language focuses on ability. Reason (R): Everyone deserves dignity.
questions.why: Both are true: respectful language focuses on ability, because everyone deserves dignity. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Correct:
questions.why: With 'she' we use 'has', and 'make' has the irregular past participle 'made'. So 'She has made many shawls' is correct.

questions.q: Embroidery is different from weaving because it …
questions.why: Embroidery decorates cloth that already exists with stitches. Weaving makes the cloth itself on a loom.

questions.q: Choose: 'She (has won / won) an award last year.'
questions.why: 'Last year' is a finished, specific time, so we use simple past 'won'. 'Has won' does not go with a fixed past time.

questions.q: Read: 'Year after year she practised, until the needle obeyed her toes.' Quality shown?
questions.why: Practising year after year until the needle obeyed her toes shows perseverance. Laziness, luck or anger do not fit.

questions.q: Mirror-work embroidery is linked with …
questions.why: Mirror-work embroidery is linked with Kutch, Gujarat. Lucknow is known for chikankari and Amritsar and Kolkata for other things.

questions.q: Which is respectful?
options: She is a poor helpless girl.
She is an artist who uses her feet to embroider.
questions.why: 'An artist who uses her feet to embroider' respects her skill. 'Cripple', 'poor helpless girl' and 'can't do anything' are insulting or untrue.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'They has shown great courage.'
questions.why: 'They' is plural, so we need 'have', and the past participle of 'show' is 'shown'. So 'They have shown great courage' is correct.

questions.q: Case: You want to write a profile of a local craftsperson. First step?
options: Copy from a website about someone else
questions.why: A profile must be accurate, so first interview the person and note real facts. Copying about someone else or inventing is wrong.

courses.note: Only the main idea of this true-life text is summarised here; read the full chapter in your Poorvi textbook for details.

courses.title: Ch 16 · National War Memorial
courses.summary: An informational text about the National War Memorial in New Delhi, which honours Indian soldiers who gave their lives in the service of the nation after Independence — its design of concentric circles, the eternal flame, Param Yoddha Sthal, and what it teaches about courage and sacrifice. Reading informational text, words for values, passive voice basics, and writing a respectful visit report.
outcomes: Learners can describe the purpose and main features of the National War Memorial
Learners can explain values such as courage, sacrifice and duty
Learners can recognise and form simple passive sentences
Learners can write a respectful report of a visit

scenes.text: Class 6 visits the National War Memorial near India Gate, New Delhi.
At the centre burns an eternal flame.
Thousands of names are engraved on granite tablets.
The children stand silently, feeling grateful.

steps.title: About the memorial
steps.body: The **National War Memorial** in New Delhi, near **India Gate**, was **inaugurated on 25 February 2019**. It honours soldiers of the Indian armed forces who laid down their lives in conflicts and operations **after Independence**.

steps.title: Design: four concentric circles
steps.body:
- **Amar Chakra** (circle of immortality) — the **eternal flame**
- **Veerta Chakra** (circle of bravery) — bronze murals of famous battles
- **Tyag Chakra** (circle of sacrifice) — names of fallen soldiers on granite tablets
- **Rakshak Chakra** (circle of protection) — rows of trees, like soldiers guarding the nation

Nearby, **Param Yoddha Sthal** has busts of the recipients of the **Param Vir Chakra**, India's highest wartime gallantry award. In 2022, the Amar Jawan Jyoti flame at India Gate was merged with the eternal flame here.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Which circle has the soldiers' names?

- **Tyag Chakra**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
What is India's highest wartime gallantry award?

- **Param Vir Chakra**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Confusing India Gate (built earlier, in memory of soldiers of World War I and other campaigns) with the National War Memorial (2019, post-Independence).

activity.prompt: Match the circle to its meaning.
pairs: Busts of Param Vir Chakra awardees

quiz.why: The National War Memorial is in New Delhi, near India Gate. It is not in Kolkata, Chennai or Mumbai.
The memorial was inaugurated on 25 February 2019. 1947 is Independence and 1971 is a war year.
The eternal flame burns in the Amar Chakra, 'amar' meaning immortal. The other circles have different features.
The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest wartime gallantry award. Padma Shri, Bharat Ratna and Arjuna Award are civilian or sports honours.
The memorial honours soldiers who died after Independence in 1947. It is not for sports or only for 1857.

story.title: A letter from a soldier's daughter

scenes.text: Nisha's father serves in the Army at a high-altitude post.
He writes about guarding the border in the cold.
Nisha feels proud and a little worried.
She learns what duty and sacrifice mean.

steps.title: Values
steps.body:
- **Courage**: acting bravely despite fear
- **Sacrifice**: giving up something precious for others
- **Duty**: doing what is expected of you responsibly
- **Gratitude**: thankfulness to those who protect us
- **Unity**: soldiers from every region serving together

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Use 'sacrifice' in a sentence.

- *The soldiers' sacrifice keeps our borders safe.*

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
How can students show gratitude to the armed forces?

- Write letters, observe silence on memorial days, respect veterans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Glorifying war — memorials honour sacrifice and remind us of the value of peace.

activity.prompt: Write a short note of thanks to the soldiers who protect our country.
activity.hint: Mention a value (courage, duty, sacrifice) and how it inspires you.

quiz.why: Courage means acting bravely even when you feel fear. Having no fear at all is not courage, and running away is the opposite.

options: giving up something precious for others
quiz.why: Sacrifice means giving up something precious, like time or life, for others. Shopping, prizes and sleeping are not sacrifice.

options: sacrifice and the value of peace
quiz.why: Memorials remind us of sacrifice and the value of peace. They are not about games or holidays.
Gratitude means thankfulness for what others have done. Jealousy and anger are different feelings.

quiz.q: A way to show respect at a memorial?
quiz.why: Standing quietly shows respect at a memorial. Climbing walls, littering or playing loud music is disrespectful.

scenes.text: The guide says, 'The names are engraved on granite.'
'Who engraved them?' asks Rohan.
Teacher: 'In passive voice, the action matters more than who did it.'
The memorial was inaugurated in 2019.

steps.title: Active vs passive
steps.body:
- **Active**: subject does the action — *Workers engraved the names.*
- **Passive**: subject receives the action — *The names **were engraved** (by workers).*
- Form: **am/is/are/was/were + past participle**
- Used when the doer is unknown or less important, common in informational writing.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Make passive: 'The Prime Minister inaugurated the memorial in 2019.'

- **The memorial was inaugurated by the Prime Minister in 2019.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Identify voice: 'Trees are planted in rows.'

- **Passive**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Wrong participle: 'was build' ✗ → 'was built' ✓

items.text: The memorial was built in New Delhi.
The flame is kept burning day and night.

quiz.why: The passive voice is formed with a form of 'be' plus the past participle, as in 'was built'. Other patterns make future or continuous forms.
'Trees' is plural, so the passive is 'were planted' (were + past participle). 'Trees was' is a mistake.

options: the doer is unknown or less important
quiz.why: The passive is useful when the doer is unknown or less important than the action. It is not for jokes or rudeness.
The passive uses 'was' with a singular subject and the past participle 'built': 'The memorial was built in 2019.' 'Build' is the wrong form.
In the active voice, the subject does the action. In the passive voice, the subject receives it.

scenes.text: After the trip, students write a report for the school magazine.
They include date, place, what they saw, what they learned.
Facts in past tense, some passive sentences.
The best report is published.

steps.title: Report format (120–150 words)
steps.body:
- **Heading** and **byline** (By Asha, Class 6B)
- **Introduction**: who, when, where, why
- **Body**: what was seen/done (in order)
- **Conclusion**: what was learned, thanks
- Past tense; formal, respectful tone

steps.title: Model opening
steps.body:
**A Visit to the National War Memorial**
*By Asha Verma, Class 6B*
*On 15 November, forty students of Class 6 visited the National War Memorial in New Delhi. We were welcomed by a guide who explained the four circles of the memorial…*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing a diary-style emotional piece instead of a factual report.

quiz.why: A report starts with a heading and a byline giving the writer's name. A poem, joke or recipe is not how a report starts.
Reports tell about things that already happened, so they are written in the past tense. Imperatives and questions are not used mainly.
A report is formal and factual, so it uses clear, serious language. Slang, anger or silliness does not suit it.
A byline shows the writer's name. The title is a different part, and the date or price is not what a byline gives.
The conclusion of a report says what was learned or the main outcome. It should not bring in a new topic.

questions.q: National War Memorial is in …
questions.why: The National War Memorial is in New Delhi, near India Gate. It is not in Jaipur, Chandigarh or Pune.

questions.q: Inaugurated on …
questions.why: The memorial was inaugurated on 25 February 2019. 15 August 1947 is Independence Day and 26 January 1950 is Republic Day.

questions.q: 'Sacrifice' means …
options: giving up something precious for others
questions.why: Sacrifice means giving up something precious for others. Winning, resting and buying do not mean this.

questions.q: Eternal flame is in the …
questions.why: The eternal flame is in the Amar Chakra, the circle of immortality. Tyag, Rakshak and Veerta Chakra are other circles.

questions.q: Passive of 'Workers built the wall.'
options: The wall was built by workers.
The wall was build by workers.
questions.why: The passive needs 'was' and the past participle 'built', and the doer follows 'by'. 'The wall was built by workers' is correct.

questions.q: Names of soldiers are on the …
questions.why: The names of the soldiers are on the Tyag Chakra, the circle of sacrifice. The other circles hold the flame, murals or trees.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The memorial honours post-Independence soldiers. Reason (R): India Gate commemorates earlier campaigns.
options: Both true, R explains why a new memorial was needed
questions.why: Both are true: the memorial honours soldiers after Independence, and India Gate commemorates earlier campaigns. That is why a new memorial was needed.

questions.q: Param Vir Chakra is …
questions.why: The Param Vir Chakra is India's highest wartime gallantry award. It is not a civilian award, festival or sports trophy.

questions.q: Which sentence is passive?
questions.why: 'The flame is kept burning' uses 'is' plus the past participle 'kept', which is the passive. The other sentences are active.

questions.q: Rakshak Chakra has …
questions.why: The Rakshak Chakra has rows of trees, which stand as a protective circle. The flame, murals and names are in other circles.

questions.q: Read: 'The visitors fell silent before the wall of names.' Inference?
questions.why: Visitors falling silent before the wall of names shows respect and emotion. The text gives no sign of anger or boredom.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'The murals was made of bronze.'
options: The murals were made of bronze.
The murals was make of bronze.
questions.why: 'Murals' is plural, so it needs 'were', not 'was'. So 'The murals were made of bronze' is correct.

questions.q: Which is suitable for a visit report?
options: On 15 November, we visited the memorial.
questions.why: A visit report is formal and in the past tense, with a date. Questions, slang and future tense do not suit it.

questions.q: Why do memorials matter for peace?
options: They remind us of the cost of war
questions.why: Memorials remind us of the cost of war, so they push us to value peace. They do not celebrate war.

questions.q: Case: A student wants to show gratitude to soldiers. Best idea?
options: Write thank-you letters through the school
questions.why: Writing thank-you letters through the school is a respectful way to show gratitude. Ignoring it, littering or playing on the memorial is disrespectful.

courses.title: Grammar for Class 6 English
courses.summary: A complete Class 6 grammar toolkit: sentences and their types, nouns and pronouns, verbs and tenses (simple present, past, future, continuous), subject–verb agreement, articles, adjectives and adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions — with practice.
outcomes: Learners can identify and use parts of speech correctly
Learners can form and use the main tenses
Learners can apply subject–verb agreement and articles
Learners can build correct sentences of different types

scenes.text: Teacher gives word cards: 'the', 'dog', 'barked'.
Students build 'The dog barked.'
Then 'Did the dog bark?' and 'Don't bark!'
Four kinds of sentences from a few words.

steps.title: Sentence types
steps.body:
- **Declarative** (statement): *The bus is late.*
- **Interrogative** (question): *Is the bus late?*
- **Imperative** (command/request): *Please wait here.*
- **Exclamatory** (strong feeling): *What a long wait!*
Every sentence has a **subject** (who/what) and a **predicate** (what is said about it).

steps.title: Nouns
steps.body:
- **Common** (city), **proper** (Chennai), **collective** (a flock of birds, a team of players), **abstract** (honesty, joy), **countable/uncountable**
- Plurals: boy–boys, box–boxes, baby–babies, leaf–leaves, child–children, mouse–mice

steps.title: Pronouns
steps.body: Replace nouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (subject) · me, him, her, us, them (object) · my/mine, your/yours … (possessive) · myself … (reflexive)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Type? 'Close the window, please.'

- **Imperative**.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Replace nouns with pronouns: 'Riya gave Arjun Riya's book.'

- *She gave **him** **her** book.*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Me and Ravi went' ✗ → 'Ravi and I went' ✓
- 'childs', 'mouses' ✗

items.text: The sun rises in the east.

quiz.why: A group of birds is called a flock. A team is for players, a herd is for cattle and a bunch is for flowers or keys.
An abstract noun names an idea or quality we cannot touch, like honesty. Dog and table are common nouns and Delhi is proper.
Words ending in -f often change to -ves in the plural, so 'leaf' becomes 'leaves'. 'Leafs' and 'leafes' are wrong.
'Ravi and I' is correct as the subject, since I is a subject pronoun and it is polite to name the other person first. 'Me' is an object pronoun.
'Them' is an object pronoun, used after verbs, as in 'I saw them'. They, we and I are subject pronouns.

scenes.text: Neel writes three lines on the board.
'Yesterday I played cricket.'
'Today I am studying.' 'I study every day.'
'Tomorrow I will visit Nani.'

steps.title: Main tenses
steps.body:
- **Simple present**: habits/facts — *She reads daily.*
- **Present continuous** (am/is/are + -ing): now — *She is reading now.*
- **Simple past**: finished — *She read yesterday.*
- **Past continuous** (was/were + -ing): in progress in the past — *She was reading when I called.*
- **Simple future** (will + base): *She will read tomorrow.*
- **Present perfect** (has/have + past participle): *She has read this book.*

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'I am go to school now.'

- **I am going to school now.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Choose: 'When the bell rang, we (were writing / wrote) a test.'

- **were writing** (in progress).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Using present continuous for habits: 'I am going to school every day' ✗ → 'I go to school every day'.

activity.prompt: Match the sentence to its tense.
pairs: She was playing when it rained.

quiz.why: Present continuous is 'is/am/are' plus -ing. For 'he' it is 'is eating'.
The simple future is 'will' plus the base verb, so 'They will go'. 'Went' and 'gone' are past forms.

options: We were watching TV when the lights went out.
quiz.why: Past continuous uses 'were' with 'we' plus -ing: 'We were watching TV when the lights went out.' 'We was' is wrong.

options: I walk to school every day.
I am walking to school every day.
quiz.why: A habit uses the simple present, as in 'I walk to school every day.' The other sentences mix tenses.
Present perfect is has/have plus the past participle: 'She has finished.' 'Yesterday' goes with simple past instead.

scenes.text: Teacher writes: 'The boys plays football.'
Ravi spots it: 'Boys play!'
Next: 'She ate a apple.' → 'an apple'.
Small words, big difference.

steps.title: Agreement
steps.body: Singular subject → singular verb (*The girl sings*); plural subject → plural verb (*The girls sing*). Watch out: *Each of the boys **is** …*, *Everyone **has** …*, *The box of pens **is** …* (subject = box).

steps.title: Articles
steps.body:
- **a** before consonant sounds (a book, a uniform — 'yoo' sound)
- **an** before vowel sounds (an apple, an hour — silent h)
- **the** for something specific or unique (the Sun, the Ganga, the book I lent you)

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'Each of the students have a book.'

- **Each of the students has a book.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Fill: ___ honest man, ___ university, ___ Himalayas

- **an**, **a**, **the**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'a hour' ✗ → 'an hour'; 'an university' ✗ → 'a university'

activity.text: She waited for ___ hour. ___ Moon looks bright tonight. He is ___ European writer.

options: The dogs is barking loudly every.
quiz.why: A plural subject 'dogs' takes a plural verb: 'The dogs bark.' 'Barks' goes with a singular subject.
Use 'an' before a vowel sound. 'Umbrella' starts with the vowel sound 'u' as in 'up', so it is 'an umbrella'.
'Uniform' begins with a 'yoo' sound, which acts like a consonant, so we say 'a uniform'. 'An' is used for vowel sounds.
'Everyone' is singular, so it takes 'has': 'Everyone has arrived.' 'Have' and 'are' are wrong.
Unique things like the Sun, the Moon and the Earth take 'the'. There is only one of them.

scenes.text: Pick a noun card: 'kite'.
Add an adjective: 'a red kite'.
Add an adverb: 'flew swiftly'.
Add a preposition and conjunction: 'over the trees and away'.

steps.title: Quick guide
steps.body:
- **Adjectives** describe nouns: big, blue, three, honest; degrees: tall–taller–tallest, good–better–best, bad–worse–worst
- **Adverbs** describe verbs/adjectives: slowly, very, often, here
- **Prepositions** show relation: in, on, at, under, between, during, since, for
- **Conjunctions** join: and, but, or, so, because, although

steps.title: Time prepositions
steps.body: **at** 5 o'clock, **on** Monday / 15 August, **in** July / 2025 / the morning

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body:
Correct: 'This is the most good book.'

- **This is the best book.**

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body:
Fill: ___ Sunday, ___ 7 pm, ___ winter

- **on**, **at**, **in**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'more better' ✗; 'in Monday' ✗ → 'on Monday'

activity.prompt: Which part of speech is the word in CAPITALS?

items.text: the cat is UNDER the bed
it rained, SO we stayed in

quiz.why: 'Good' has irregular forms: better, best. So the superlative is 'best', not 'goodest'.
We use 'on' with days: 'on Monday'. 'At' is for clock times and 'in' is for months or years.
We use 'at' with clock times: 'at 6 o'clock'. 'On' is for days and 'in' is for months.
'Bad' is irregular: bad, worse, worst. So the comparative is 'worse'; 'worst' is the superlative.
A conjunction joins words or clauses, and 'because' joins a reason to a result. 'Happy' is an adjective, 'quickly' an adverb and 'under' a preposition.

questions.q: Plural of 'child'?
questions.why: 'Child' has an irregular plural: 'children'. 'Childrens' wrongly adds -s to an already plural word.

questions.q: Article: ___ hour
questions.why: The 'h' in 'hour' is silent, so the word starts with a vowel sound and takes 'an': 'an hour'.

questions.q: Interrogative sentence?
questions.why: An interrogative sentence asks a question, and 'Where do you live?' does that. 'What a house!' is an exclamation and 'Live here!' is a command.

questions.q: Past of 'write'?
questions.why: 'Write' is irregular: write, wrote, written. The simple past is 'wrote'.

questions.q: Collective noun: a ___ of cows
questions.why: A group of cows is a herd. A swarm is for insects, a flock for birds or sheep and a pack for wolves.

questions.q: Correct:
questions.why: Present continuous is 'is/am/are' plus -ing, and 'she' takes 'is': 'She is reading now.' 'She are' is wrong.

questions.q: '___ July'
questions.why: We use 'in' with months: 'in July'. 'On' is for days and dates, and 'at' for clock times.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'Each of the girls has a pen' is correct. Reason (R): 'Each' takes a singular verb.
questions.why: Both are true: 'each' is singular, so it takes 'has'. The reason explains why the assertion is correct.

questions.q: Superlative of 'beautiful'?
questions.why: Long adjectives like 'beautiful' use 'most' for the superlative. 'Beautifulest' and 'beautifuler' are wrong.

questions.q: Which is an abstract noun?
questions.why: 'Kindness' is a quality we cannot touch, so it is an abstract noun. Kolkata is proper, and teacher and chair are common nouns.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'I am knowing the answer.'
questions.why: 'Know' is a stative verb, which is not normally used in continuous form. So we say 'I know the answer.'

questions.q: Choose: 'While I ___ , the phone rang.'
questions.why: A longer action in progress (cooking) is interrupted by a short one (the phone rang), so we use past continuous 'was cooking'.

questions.q: Correct:
options: The box of pencils were on desk.
The box of pencils are on the desk.
The box of pencils is on the desk.
questions.why: The subject is 'box', which is singular, not 'pencils'. So the verb is 'is': 'The box of pencils is on the desk.'

questions.q: Which sentence has an adjective, an adverb and a preposition?
options: The small dog ran quickly under the table.
questions.why: 'Small' is an adjective, 'quickly' an adverb and 'under' a preposition, so this sentence has all three. The others are shorter.

questions.q: Pick the correct article set: '___ elephant and ___ unicorn walked to ___ river.'
questions.why: 'Elephant' and 'unicorn' differ in sound: 'an elephant' (vowel sound), 'a unicorn' (yoo sound). 'The river' is a specific river.

courses.title: Writing Skills for Class 6
courses.summary: The writing formats expected in Class 6: paragraphs, notices, informal and formal letters, diary entries and short stories — with models, checklists and practice.
outcomes: Learners can write well-organised paragraphs
Learners can write notices in the correct format
Learners can write informal and formal letters
Learners can write diary entries and short stories

scenes.text: Aarav loses his blue water bottle in the playground.
He writes a notice for the school board.
Title, date, details, contact — all in a box.
His bottle is returned the next day.

steps.title: Notice format (≤ 50 words, in a box)
steps.body:
- Name of school/organisation
- **NOTICE**
- Date
- Heading (LOST / SPORTS DAY / ART COMPETITION)
- Body: what, when, where, who to contact
- Name and designation of writer

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
**ABC Public School, Pune**
**NOTICE**
12 November 2026
**LOST WATER BOTTLE**
A blue steel water bottle with a dolphin sticker was lost in the playground on 11 November. The finder is requested to return it to the undersigned or the class teacher of 6B.
Aarav Mehta, Class 6B

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing a long story; notices are short and factual.

quiz.why: A notice is short, about 50 words, so it can be read quickly. A very long notice would defeat its purpose.
A notice is written inside a box so that it stands out. It is not put in a circle or bubble.
A notice must have a heading (NOTICE and title) and a date. Poems and jokes do not belong in it.
A notice is formal and factual, giving clear information. Angry, chatty or poetic tones do not suit it.
A notice is signed by the writer along with their designation, so readers know who issued it. A random person or nobody cannot.

scenes.text: Nidhi writes to her cousin about her new puppy — chatty and warm.
Then she writes to the principal asking for leave — polite and formal.
Different readers, different formats.
Both letters get happy replies.

steps.title: Informal letter (to family/friends)
steps.body: Sender's address → date → 'Dear Riya,' → body (news, questions, feelings) → closing 'Yours lovingly,' → name.

steps.title: Formal letter (to principal/officials)
