steps.body: Sender's address → date → receiver's designation and address → **Subject:** → 'Respected Sir/Madam,' → body (purpose, details, request) → 'Thanking you, Yours obediently/sincerely,' → name, class/roll no.

steps.title: Formal model (leave)
steps.body:
*Subject: Application for two days' leave*
*Respected Madam,*
*I am Nidhi Rao of Class 6B. I request leave on 20 and 21 November as I have to attend my cousin's wedding in Jaipur. I shall complete the missed work. Kindly grant me leave.*
*Thanking you,*
*Yours obediently, Nidhi Rao, 6B, Roll No. 18*

steps.title: Informal opening
steps.body: *Dear Kabir, I hope you're doing well! Guess what — we have a puppy named Laddoo…*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Using slang in formal letters; missing the subject line.

items.text: Subject: Request for a library card

quiz.why: A subject line is part of a formal letter and tells the reader the topic. Informal letters, diaries and poems do not need one.
A principal is addressed with respect, so 'Respected Sir/Madam' is right. 'Hi there', 'Hey' or 'Dear buddy' are too casual.
An informal letter to someone close ends warmly, like 'Yours lovingly'. 'Yours obediently' and 'Thanking you' are formal.

options: brief, polite and to the point
quiz.why: Formal letters should be brief, polite and to the point. Slang, rhyme and long chatty writing do not suit them.
In a letter, the date comes after the sender's address. It is not in the subject or only at the end.

scenes.text: After her first stage performance, Mira opens her diary.
She writes how nervous she was backstage.
And how the applause felt.
Diaries help us understand our feelings.

steps.title: Diary format (80–100 words)
steps.body: Date (day) → 'Dear Diary,' → what happened → feelings and thoughts → (optional) what you'll do next → signature/name. First person, mostly past tense, personal tone.

steps.title: Model
steps.body:
*Friday, 14 November 2026*
*Dear Diary,*
*Today was Children's Day and I recited a poem on stage! My knees were shaking backstage, but when I saw Ma in the front row, I felt brave. I forgot one line, yet I carried on, and everyone clapped. I learned that mistakes are okay. Next time, I'll practise in front of the mirror.*
*Mira*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Writing only events without feelings.

quiz.why: A diary records your own thoughts, so it is written in first person with 'I'. Third person is for other people's stories.
A diary entry includes the writer's feelings, since it is personal. A subject line or notice box belongs to other formats.
A diary entry begins with the date and 'Dear Diary'. 'Respected Sir' and 'NOTICE' belong to other formats.
A diary tells what happened during the day, so it is mainly in the past tense. It is not passive or imperative.
A diary lets you reflect personally on your day and feelings. It is not for ordering food or informing the school.

scenes.text: Prompt: 'One morning, a small box appeared on my doorstep.'
Isha brainstorms: who left it? What's inside?
She plans beginning, problem, climax and ending.
Her story about a lost kitten wins the class prize.

steps.title: From prompt to story (120–150 words)
steps.body:
- Use the given opening/outline
- Add a title
- Beginning (who, where) → problem → rising action → climax → resolution
- Dialogue, vivid verbs, past tense
- Optional moral

steps.title: Outline to story
steps.body:
Outline: *boy finds wallet — owner's card inside — returns it — reward refused.*

Start: *Ravi spotted a brown wallet near the bus stop. Inside were ₹2,000 and a card with a name: R. Singh…*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Ignoring the given outline points; every point must be used.

quiz.q: A story from an outline must …
quiz.why: When a story is written from an outline, it must use all the given points. Ignoring them or writing one line does not answer the task.
The climax is the most exciting turning point of a story. The moral and title are different parts.
Stories tell what has happened, so they are usually in the past tense. Imperative and future are not normal for narration.
A title should fit the story, giving a hint of what it is about. A date or a random title does not help.
Good stories use vivid verbs and dialogue to make scenes lively. Tables, lists or only nouns do not tell a story.

questions.q: A notice is written in a …
questions.why: A notice is written inside a box so it stands out. A circle, bubble or triangle is not used.

questions.q: Diary entries begin with …
questions.why: A diary entry begins with the date and 'Dear Diary'. 'Respected Madam', a subject line or 'NOTICE' belong to other formats.

questions.q: Formal letter salutation?
questions.why: A formal letter is addressed respectfully, so 'Respected Sir' fits. 'Hi', 'Hey dude' and 'Dear friend' are casual.

questions.q: A subject line is needed in …
questions.why: A subject line is needed in formal letters. Stories, diaries and informal letters do not need one.

questions.q: Notice word limit?
questions.why: A notice should be short, about 50 words. 200 or 500 words is too long, and 10 words is too little.

questions.q: Informal letter closing?
questions.why: An informal letter to a close person ends warmly, like 'Yours lovingly'. The other closings are formal.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Diary entries include feelings. Reason (R): A diary is a personal record.
questions.why: Both are true: a diary includes feelings because it is a personal record. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which belongs in a notice?
questions.why: A notice carries the date, heading and contact details so people can act on it. A poem, slang or secrets do not belong.

questions.q: Which is the correct order in a formal letter?
options: Sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation
questions.why: A formal letter goes in order: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation. The other orders are wrong.

questions.q: Which line suits a formal letter?
options: I request you to kindly grant me leave.
questions.why: 'I request you to kindly grant me leave' is polite and formal. Slang and rude lines do not suit a formal letter.

questions.q: Case: You found a gold-coloured pen in the library. Best writing format to inform the school?
questions.why: To inform the whole school about a found item, write a notice. It is short, formal and public, unlike a poem, diary or informal letter.

questions.q: Case: You want to tell your grandmother about your sports day. Format?
questions.why: A grandmother is a close person, so an informal letter is the right choice. A formal letter, notice or report would be too stiff.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of a notice?
questions.why: 'Dear Diary' belongs in a diary entry, not in a notice. A notice has a date, heading and the writer's name.

questions.q: Best opening for a story from the prompt 'The lights went out suddenly…'
options: The lights went out suddenly, and a strange humming filled the room.
questions.why: A good story opening makes the reader curious, and 'The lights went out suddenly, and a strange humming filled the room' sets a scene. The other options do not.

questions.q: Case: A formal letter has no subject line and ends 'Love, Riya'. What should be fixed?
options: Add a subject and use a formal closing
questions.why: A formal letter needs a subject line and a formal closing, not 'Love, Riya'. Fixing these makes it correct.

courses.title: हिंदी व्याकरण की नींव · Hindi Grammar Basics (Class 6)
courses.summary: कक्षा 6 के लिए हिंदी व्याकरण की नींव: वर्ण (स्वर-व्यंजन), संज्ञा और उसके भेद, सर्वनाम, लिंग और वचन, क्रिया, विशेषण, काल, तथा पर्यायवाची और विलोम शब्द — सरल उदाहरणों और अभ्यास के साथ।
outcomes: विद्यार्थी स्वर और व्यंजन पहचान सकते हैं
विद्यार्थी संज्ञा के भेद, सर्वनाम, लिंग और वचन सही प्रयोग कर सकते हैं
विद्यार्थी क्रिया, विशेषण और काल पहचान व प्रयोग कर सकते हैं
विद्यार्थी पर्यायवाची और विलोम शब्दों से भाषा समृद्ध कर सकते हैं

scenes.text: दादी ने अनु को चॉक से 'अ, आ, इ, ई' लिखकर दिखाया।
फिर 'क, ख, ग, घ' — 'ये व्यंजन हैं,' दादी बोलीं।
'स्वर अपने आप बोले जाते हैं, व्यंजन स्वर की मदद से।'
अनु ने अपना नाम वर्णों में तोड़कर लिखा: अ + न् + उ।

steps.title: वर्ण
steps.body: भाषा की सबसे छोटी ध्वनि जिसके टुकड़े न हो सकें, **वर्ण** कहलाती है। वर्णों के समूह को **वर्णमाला** कहते हैं।

steps.title: स्वर
steps.body: जो वर्ण बिना किसी दूसरे वर्ण की सहायता के बोले जाते हैं: **अ, आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ऋ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ** (11 स्वर)। इनके चिह्न **मात्राएँ** कहलाते हैं: ा ि ी ु ू ृ े ै ो ौ।

steps.title: व्यंजन
steps.body: जो वर्ण स्वर की सहायता से बोले जाते हैं: क-वर्ग (क ख ग घ ङ), च-वर्ग, ट-वर्ग, त-वर्ग, प-वर्ग, तथा य र ल व, श ष स ह। **संयुक्त व्यंजन**: क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र।

steps.title: उदाहरण 1
steps.body:
'कमल' के वर्ण अलग कीजिए।

- क् + अ + म् + अ + ल् + अ

steps.title: उदाहरण 2
steps.body:
'ज्ञान' में कौन-सा संयुक्त व्यंजन है?

- **ज्ञ** (ज् + ञ)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'ऋ' को व्यंजन मानना — यह स्वर है।
- मात्रा गलत लगाना: 'दिवार' ✗ → 'दीवार' ✓

quiz.q: हिंदी में मूल स्वर कितने माने जाते हैं?
quiz.why: हिंदी में मूल स्वर 11 माने जाते हैं: अ, आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ऋ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ। 33 व्यंजनों की संख्या है, और 52 कुल वर्णों की गिनती में आती है।
'क्ष' दो व्यंजनों क् + ष से बना है, इसलिए यह संयुक्त व्यंजन है। यह न स्वर है, न मात्रा।
'ी' दीर्घ स्वर 'ई' की मात्रा है। 'इ' की मात्रा 'ि' होती है।

quiz.q: वर्णों के समूह को कहते हैं …
quiz.why: वर्णों के समूह को वर्णमाला कहते हैं। शब्दकोश, पद और वाक्य अलग चीज़ें हैं।
'ग' व्यंजन है, जबकि ओ, ऐ और आ स्वर हैं।

scenes.text: रवि अपने मित्र के साथ आगरा के मेले में गया।
उसने मिठाई खरीदी और झूले पर बैठा।
उसे बहुत खुशी हुई।
अध्यापिका ने पूछा: इसमें संज्ञा शब्द कौन-से हैं?

steps.title: संज्ञा
steps.body:
किसी व्यक्ति, वस्तु, स्थान, भाव के नाम को **संज्ञा** कहते हैं।

- **व्यक्तिवाचक**: विशेष नाम — रवि, आगरा, गंगा
- **जातिवाचक**: पूरी जाति का नाम — लड़का, शहर, नदी, मिठाई
- **भाववाचक**: भाव/गुण — खुशी, ईमानदारी, बचपन, मिठास

steps.title: सर्वनाम
steps.body: संज्ञा के स्थान पर आने वाले शब्द: मैं, तुम, आप, वह, यह, हम, वे, कोई, कुछ, कौन, अपना।

steps.title: लिंग और वचन
steps.body:
- **लिंग**: पुल्लिंग (लड़का, घोड़ा, शेर) / स्त्रीलिंग (लड़की, घोड़ी, शेरनी)
- **वचन**: एकवचन (लड़का, किताब) / बहुवचन (लड़के, किताबें)

steps.title: उदाहरण 1
steps.body:
'रवि को मेले में बहुत खुशी हुई।' संज्ञा पहचानें।

- रवि (व्यक्तिवाचक), मेले (जातिवाचक), खुशी (भाववाचक)

steps.title: उदाहरण 2
steps.body:
बहुवचन बनाइए: नदी, कपड़ा, माला

- **नदियाँ, कपड़े, मालाएँ**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - 'किताबों' और 'किताबें' का भ्रम: 'किताबें मेज़ पर हैं' (कर्ता), 'किताबों को रखो' (कारक के साथ)।

quiz.why: 'ईमानदारी' किसी व्यक्ति के गुण या भाव को बताती है, इसलिए यह भाववाचक संज्ञा है। जातिवाचक या व्यक्तिवाचक नहीं है।
'गंगा' एक विशेष नदी का नाम है, इसलिए यह व्यक्तिवाचक संज्ञा है। जातिवाचक संज्ञा पूरी जाति का नाम होती है, जैसे 'नदी'।
'वह' संज्ञा के स्थान पर आता है, इसलिए यह सर्वनाम है। यह न क्रिया है, न विशेषण।
'नदी' का बहुवचन 'नदियाँ' होता है, क्योंकि ई की जगह 'इयाँ' लगता है। 'नदीयाँ' लिखना गलत है।
'मोर' का स्त्रीलिंग 'मोरनी' है। मोरिन या मोराइन जैसे रूप सही नहीं हैं।

scenes.text: सुबह सुंदर फूल खिले।
छोटी चिड़िया मीठा गीत गा रही थी।
सीमा तेज़ी से दौड़ी और पौधों को पानी दिया।
अध्यापक ने कहा: 'खिले, गा रही थी, दौड़ी — ये क्रियाएँ हैं।'

steps.title: क्रिया
steps.body: जिस शब्द से किसी काम का करना या होना पता चले: खाना, पढ़ना, दौड़ना, सोना, खिलना।

steps.title: विशेषण
steps.body: संज्ञा या सर्वनाम की विशेषता बताने वाले शब्द: सुंदर फूल, **छोटी** चिड़िया, **तीन** केले, **मीठा** आम। जिसकी विशेषता बताई जाए वह **विशेष्य** है।

steps.title: उदाहरण 1
steps.body:
'लाल गुलाब महक रहा है।' विशेषण और क्रिया बताइए।

- विशेषण: **लाल**; क्रिया: **महक रहा है**

steps.title: उदाहरण 2
steps.body:
भविष्यत् काल में बदलें: 'मैं पुस्तक पढ़ता हूँ।'

- **मैं पुस्तक पढ़ूँगा।**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - विशेषण का लिंग-वचन संज्ञा के अनुसार: 'अच्छी लड़का' ✗ → 'अच्छा लड़का' ✓

quiz.why: क्रिया वह शब्द है जो काम को बताता है, और 'दौड़ना' एक काम है। 'लड़का' संज्ञा है, 'वह' सर्वनाम है और 'सुंदर' विशेषण है।
'मीठा' आम की विशेषता बताता है, इसलिए यह विशेषण है। 'आम' संज्ञा है।

quiz.q: 'हम कल जाएँगे' किस काल में है?
quiz.why: 'कल जाएँगे' आने वाले समय की बात है, इसलिए यह भविष्यत् काल है। बीता समय भूतकाल और अभी का समय वर्तमान काल होता है।
विशेषण का लिंग संज्ञा के अनुसार होता है। 'लड़का' पुल्लिंग है, इसलिए 'अच्छा लड़का' सही है।
'गाया' काम हो चुके होने को बताता है, इसलिए यह भूतकाल का वाक्य है। यह वर्तमान या भविष्य का नहीं है।

scenes.text: अध्यापिका ने कहा: 'सूरज के कई नाम हैं — सूर्य, रवि, दिनकर।'
'और रात का उल्टा?' — 'दिन!'
बच्चों ने शब्दों की एक तालिका बनाई।
अब उनके निबंध और सुंदर हो गए।

steps.title: पर्यायवाची
steps.body:
समान अर्थ वाले शब्द:

- सूर्य — रवि, दिनकर, भानु
- पानी — जल, नीर, वारि
- पेड़ — वृक्ष, तरु, विटप
- माँ — माता, जननी, अम्बा
- आकाश — गगन, नभ, अंबर

steps.title: विलोम
steps.body: उल्टे अर्थ वाले शब्द: दिन–रात, सुख–दुख, आना–जाना, सच–झूठ, अमीर–गरीब, प्रकाश–अंधकार, जीत–हार, आरंभ–अंत

steps.title: उदाहरण 1
steps.body:
'जल' का एक पर्यायवाची?

- **नीर**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - पर्यायवाची हर वाक्य में बिल्कुल एक-से नहीं जमते; संदर्भ देखें।

quiz.why: 'सूर्य' का पर्यायवाची 'रवि' है। नभ, तारा और चंद्र दूसरे अर्थ के शब्द हैं।
'अमीर' का विलोम (उलटा) 'गरीब' है। राजा, सेठ और धनी अमीर के समान अर्थ वाले हैं।
'वृक्ष' का अर्थ पेड़ है। नदी, पहाड़ और फूल दूसरी चीज़ें हैं।
'आना' का विलोम 'जाना' है, क्योंकि दोनों के अर्थ उलटे हैं। गाना, खाना और पाना उलटे अर्थ वाले नहीं हैं।
'गगन' का पर्यायवाची 'आकाश' है, और 'नभ' भी इसी का रूप है। पानी, आग और धरती दूसरे अर्थ के शब्द हैं।

questions.q: हिंदी में मूल स्वर कितने?
questions.why: हिंदी में मूल स्वर 11 हैं: अ से औ तक। 33 व्यंजन होते हैं, इसलिए 33 सही उत्तर नहीं है।

questions.q: 'आगरा' कौन-सी संज्ञा है?
questions.why: 'आगरा' एक विशेष स्थान का नाम है, इसलिए यह व्यक्तिवाचक संज्ञा है। यह किसी गुण या पूरी जाति का नाम नहीं है।

questions.q: 'दिन' का विलोम?
questions.why: 'दिन' का विलोम 'रात' है, क्योंकि दोनों के अर्थ उलटे हैं। सुबह, दोपहर और शाम दिन के हिस्से हैं।
'मैं' संज्ञा की जगह आने वाला शब्द है, इसलिए यह सर्वनाम है। यह विशेषण, क्रिया या संज्ञा नहीं है।

questions.q: 'घोड़ा' का स्त्रीलिंग?
questions.why: 'घोड़ा' का स्त्रीलिंग 'घोड़ी' है। घोड़नी या घोड़िन जैसे रूप सही नहीं हैं।

questions.q: 'बचपन' कौन-सी संज्ञा है?
questions.why: 'बचपन' अवस्था को बताता है, इसलिए यह भाववाचक संज्ञा है। यह किसी व्यक्ति या जाति का नाम नहीं है।

questions.q: 'पानी' का पर्यायवाची?
questions.why: 'पानी' का पर्यायवाची 'जल' है। अग्नि, पवन और धरा पानी के समान अर्थ वाले नहीं हैं।

questions.q: कथन (A): 'ऋ' स्वर है। कारण (R): 'ऋ' बिना दूसरे वर्ण की सहायता के बोला जाता है।
options: दोनों सही, R, A की व्याख्या करता है
questions.why: दोनों कथन सही हैं: 'ऋ' स्वर है, क्योंकि स्वर बिना किसी दूसरे वर्ण की सहायता के बोला जाता है। कारण से स्वर की परिभाषा मिलती है, जो कथन की व्याख्या करती है।

questions.q: 'तीन केले' में विशेषण?
questions.why: 'तीन' केले की संख्या बताता है, इसलिए यह संख्यावाचक विशेषण है। 'केले' संज्ञा है।

questions.q: 'किताब' का बहुवचन?
questions.why: 'किताब' स्त्रीलिंग संज्ञा है, जिसका बहुवचन 'किताबें' होता है। 'किताबों' विभक्ति लगने पर आता है।

questions.q: भविष्यत् काल का वाक्य?
questions.why: 'वह कल आएगा' आने वाले समय की बात है, इसलिए यह भविष्यत् काल का वाक्य है। 'आया' बीता समय और 'आता है' वर्तमान काल है।

questions.q: सही वाक्य चुनिए।
questions.why: 'लड़की' स्त्रीलिंग और एकवचन है, इसलिए क्रिया 'गा रही है' होगी। लिंग-वचन मेल से 'सुंदर लड़की गा रही है' सही है।

questions.q: 'ज्ञ' किन वर्णों से बना है?
questions.why: 'ज्ञ' ज् और ञ से मिलकर बना संयुक्त व्यंजन है। 'क्ष' क् और ष से बनता है।

questions.q: 'मैं पत्र लिखता हूँ' का भूतकाल?
questions.why: भूतकाल का मतलब बीता हुआ समय है, इसलिए 'मैंने पत्र लिखा' सही है। 'लिख रहा हूँ' वर्तमान काल और 'लिखूँगा' भविष्यत् काल है।

questions.q: 'ईमानदार' से भाववाचक संज्ञा?
questions.why: गुणवाचक शब्द 'ईमानदार' से भाववाचक संज्ञा 'ईमानदारी' बनती है। 'ईमानदारी' गुण का भाव बताती है।

questions.q: गलत जोड़ी पहचानिए।
questions.why: सुख और आनंद के अर्थ समान हैं, इसलिए ये पर्यायवाची हैं, विलोम नहीं। इसलिए 'विलोम' वाली जोड़ी गलत है।

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 6 English
courses.summary: Revision of all 16 Poorvi chapters by unit, a grammar and writing formula sheet, reading-comprehension practice with unseen passages, and two mock papers.
outcomes: Learners can recall themes, devices and key ideas of each unit
Learners can apply grammar rules accurately
Learners can answer unseen-passage questions
Learners can attempt full mock papers

scenes.text: Isha draws a wheel with five spokes — one for each unit.
On each spoke: chapters, theme, one literary device.
She spins it and quizzes herself.
Five units, one picture.

steps.title: Units
steps.body:
- **Fables & folk tales** (A Bottle of Dew, The Raven and the Fox, Rama to the Rescue): morals, hard work, flattery, quick thinking · devices: moral, rhyme, narrative poem
- **Friendship** (The Unlikely Best Friends, A Friend's Prayer, The Chair): trust, difference, wishes, memories · devices: simile/metaphor, symbol
- **Nurturing nature** (Neem Baba, What a Bird Thought, Spices that Heal Us): respect for nature, widening perspective, traditional knowledge · devices: personification, repetition
- **Sports & wellness** (Change of Heart, The Winner, Yoga—A Way of Life): sportsmanship, perseverance, wellbeing · devices: alliteration, contrast
- **Culture & tradition** (Hamara Bharat—Incredible India!, The Kites, Ila Sachani, National War Memorial): diversity, festivals, determination, sacrifice · devices: imagery, onomatopoeia

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body:
Device in 'The old tree watched over the village'?

- **Personification**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Mixing up simile (like/as) and metaphor; alliteration (start sounds) and rhyme (end sounds).

quiz.why: 'As brave as a lion' compares two things using 'as', so it is a simile. A metaphor says one thing is another without 'like' or 'as'.
The poem shows the bird's view of the world widening as it sees more. So the theme is widening understanding, not war, sports or cooking.
'Buzz' imitates a sound, so it is onomatopoeia. It is not a comparison or a symbol.
The fox flatters the raven to get its cheese, so the lesson is to beware of flatterers. Foxes should not be trusted blindly.

options: soldiers who gave their lives after Independence
quiz.why: The National War Memorial honours soldiers who gave their lives after Independence. It is not for athletes, kings or artists.

scenes.text: Kabir writes every rule on one card.
He reads it on the bus each morning.
By exam week, he knows it by heart.
His grammar marks shoot up.

steps.title: Grammar
steps.body:
- Tenses: present simple (habits), continuous (now), past, past continuous, future (will), present perfect (has/have + pp)
- Agreement: singular subject + singular verb; each/everyone → singular
- Articles: a (consonant sound), an (vowel sound), the (specific/unique)
- Countable (many) / uncountable (much); modals + base verb; passive = be + pp
- Adverbs -ly; good → well; comparatives/superlatives (good-better-best)
- Direct speech punctuation; capitals for proper nouns; conjunctions because/so/although

steps.title: Writing
steps.body: - Notice (≤ 50 words, box) · Informal letter (Dear…, Yours lovingly) · Formal letter (Subject, Respected Sir/Madam, Yours obediently) · Diary (date, Dear Diary, feelings) · Paragraph (topic sentence + support + conclusion) · Story (title, problem, climax, resolution) · Brochure/poster (slogan, facts, call to action) · Report (heading, byline, past tense)

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body:
Correct: 'Does she likes yoga?'

- **Does she like yoga?**

steps.title: - Double comparatives · 'Although…but' · 'a hour' · missing subject line in formal letters · wrong past participles
steps.body: Top 5 slips

activity.prompt: Match the writing task to its key feature.

quiz.why: With 'she', present perfect uses 'has' plus the past participle 'gone'. 'Has went' and 'she gone' are wrong.
'Honest' starts with a silent h, so it begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an': 'an honest girl'.
A formal letter ends with a polite closing like 'Yours obediently'. 'Love' and 'Yours lovingly' are for close people.
The passive is 'be' plus the past participle, so 'The cake was baked' is passive. 'She baked a cake' is active.
'Water' is uncountable, so we say 'how much water'. 'Waters' and 'how many' do not fit.

scenes.text: In the exam, Riya gets a passage she has never seen.
She skims it first, then reads the questions.
She scans for answers and underlines clue lines.
She finishes with time to check.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
- Skim for the main idea
- Read questions; underline key words
- Scan the passage for each answer
- For vocabulary questions, use context
- For inference, quote a clue

steps.title: Passage
steps.body:
*Every winter, thousands of migratory birds fly from cold northern lands to India's lakes and wetlands. Places like Bharatpur in Rajasthan and Chilika Lake in Odisha become noisy with honks and calls. The birds find warmth and food here. When spring arrives, they begin their long journey home.*

- Main idea: **Migratory birds visit India in winter.**
- Why do they come? **Warmth and food.**
- Word meaning 'moving from one place to another seasonally': **migratory**

steps.title: Answering
steps.body: Write complete, short answers in your own words where asked; don't copy long lines.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Answering from memory instead of the passage.

activity.prompt: Order the strategy for an unseen passage.
items: Skim the passage for the main idea
Read the questions and underline key words
Scan the passage for each answer

quiz.q: First step with an unseen passage?
quiz.why: With an unseen passage, first skim to get the main idea, then read closely. Writing answers at once or copying will not help.

quiz.q: In the passage, birds come to India for …
quiz.why: The passage says birds come to India for warmth and food, which is why they migrate. Snow and mountains are what they leave behind.
Chilika Lake is in Odisha. It is not in Punjab, Rajasthan or Kerala.

quiz.q: Vocabulary questions are best solved by …
quiz.why: Vocabulary questions are best solved using the context around the word. Random guessing or the title alone is less reliable.
An inference needs a clue from the text, so we can support the answer. Guesses with no reason are not inferences.

scenes.text: Mock 1: reading, grammar, writing, literature — 2 hours.
Isha checks errors in tense and articles.
Mock 2 a week later: fewer mistakes.
She's exam-ready.

steps.title: Mock 1 — sample answers
steps.body:
- *Grammar*: 'Each of the players has a kit.' (singular)
- *Writing (notice)*: boxed, date, heading 'INTER-CLASS QUIZ', details, contact
- *Literature*: Moral of A Bottle of Dew — hard work and patience bring real wealth
- *Poem device*: 'Brave birds battle the breeze' — alliteration

steps.title: Mock 2 — sample answers
steps.body:
- *Grammar*: 'The memorial was inaugurated in 2019.' (passive)
- *Writing (formal letter)*: subject line 'Request to start a yoga club'
- *Literature*: In 'What a Bird Thought', the bird's world grows from shell to nest to leaves to sky
- *Vocabulary*: antonym of 'victory' — defeat

steps.title: Time plan
steps.body: Reading 20%, grammar 25%, writing 30%, literature 25% of your time; keep 10 minutes to revise.

items: I revised all five units' themes
I practised one notice, one letter and one diary entry
I did one unseen passage under time
I slept well the night before

quiz.why: 'She' is third person singular, so present simple takes 'goes'. 'Go' is for I/you/we/they.
The prefix 'im-' is used before words starting with p, so the opposite of 'patient' is 'impatient'. The other forms are not words.
Wind cannot whisper, as that is a human action, so giving it to the wind is personification. It is not a comparison with 'like' or 'as'.

quiz.q: Mock: Format for informing the school about a lost item?
quiz.why: A notice is the right format to inform the school about a lost item. A poem, diary or brochure would not do this job.

quiz.q: Mock: Correct passive of 'They planted trees.'
quiz.why: 'Trees' is plural, so the passive is 'were planted'. 'Trees was planted' is a mistake.
Poems like 'The Winner' are about perseverance and inner victory. Weather, travel and cooking are not their themes.

questions.q: A simile uses …
questions.why: A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'. Verbs like 'was' or 'is' do not make a simile.

questions.q: Past of 'see'?
questions.why: 'See' is irregular: see, saw, seen. The simple past is 'saw'.

questions.q: Article: ___ apple
questions.why: 'Apple' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an': 'an apple'.

questions.q: Antonym of 'success'?
questions.why: The opposite of 'success' is 'failure'. Win, victory and gain mean something like success.

questions.q: 'The leaves danced in the wind' is …
questions.why: Leaves cannot dance, as dancing is a human action, so this is personification. It is not a plain fact.

questions.q: Correct:
questions.why: With 'he' we use 'doesn't' plus the base verb: 'He doesn't like spinach.' 'Doesn't likes' repeats the -s.

questions.q: Formal letters include a …
questions.why: A formal letter has a subject line telling the topic. A byline is for reports and 'Dear Diary' is for diaries.

questions.q: Plural of 'mouse'?
questions.why: 'Mouse' has an irregular plural: 'mice'. 'Mouses' and 'mices' are wrong.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'Yoga improves flexibility' uses the present simple. Reason (R): Present simple is used for general facts.
questions.why: Both are true: 'Yoga improves flexibility' is a general fact, and present simple is used for general facts. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is alliteration?
questions.why: 'Seven silly snakes' repeats the s sound at the start of words, which is alliteration. The others do not repeat starting sounds the same way.

questions.q: Choose: 'Although it was raining, ___'
questions.why: 'Although' already shows contrast, so no 'but' or 'so' is added: 'Although it was raining, we played outside.'

questions.q: Correct: 'She has ___ (write) a letter.'
questions.why: 'Has' needs a past participle. The past participle of 'write' is 'written'. 'Wrote' is the simple past and 'writed' is wrong.

questions.q: Read: 'Meena's eyes sparkled as she unwrapped the gift.' She felt …
questions.why: Her eyes sparkled as she unwrapped the gift, so she was delighted. Scared, bored or angry do not match sparkling eyes.

questions.q: Correct the error: 'The team of players are ready.'
options: The team of players is ready.
The team of players were ready.
questions.why: The subject is 'team', which is singular, not 'players'. So the verb is 'is': 'The team of players is ready.'

questions.q: Which belongs in a diary entry?
options: I felt nervous but proud today.
questions.why: A diary is personal and uses first person feelings, like 'I felt nervous but proud today.' 'NOTICE', 'Respected Sir' and 'Subject' belong to other formats.

questions.q: Best slogan for a tree-planting poster?
questions.why: A good slogan is catchy and positive, and 'Plant a tree, breathe free!' rhymes and gives a reason. The others are dull or against trees.

questions.q: Combine using 'because': He was late. The bus broke down.
options: He was late so because the bus.
Because he was late the bus broke.
He was late because the bus broke down.
questions.why: 'Because' introduces the reason, so the result comes first: 'He was late because the bus broke down.' The other options are muddled.

questions.q: Which sentence has a metaphor and correct capitals?
options: Mumbai is a city that never sleeps.
questions.why: 'Mumbai is a city that never sleeps' calls the city a sleepless thing directly, so it is a metaphor, and 'Mumbai' has its capital. The others have errors or use 'like'.

questions.q: Passive of 'The children cleaned the park.'
options: The park was cleaned by the children.
The park were cleaned by children.
questions.why: In the passive, the object 'park' becomes the subject with 'was cleaned' and the doer follows 'by'. 'The park was cleaned by the children' is correct.

questions.q: Case: A friend writes, 'Dear Diary, Subject: My day. Yours obediently.' What's wrong?
questions.why: The letter starts like a diary ('Dear Diary') but also has a subject line and a formal closing. Mixing diary and formal-letter formats is the error.

school-c6-maths.title: Class 6 Maths · Ganita Prakash
school-c6-maths.description: Every chapter of Class 6 mathematics (Ganita Prakash, NCERT 2024 edition onward), explained from scratch with solved examples, common mistakes, quizzes, chapter tests and full mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Patterns in Mathematics
courses.summary: What mathematics really is — the search for patterns and the reasons behind them. Famous number sequences (odd, even, triangular, square, cube, Virahanka numbers, powers of 2), seeing sequences as pictures, how sequences are related, and patterns in shapes.
outcomes: Learners can recognise, extend and name the common number sequences
Learners can draw dot pictures for triangular and square numbers and explain why they work
Learners can explain relations such as 'adding odd numbers gives squares'
Learners can find number patterns hidden in shape sequences

scenes.text: Kabir collects stamps and lines them up: 1 stamp, then 3, then 6, then 10…
His sister asks, 'How many in the next row?' Kabir is stuck.
He notices the jumps: +2, +3, +4… so the next jump is +5.
1, 3, 6, 10, 15! Spotting the rule is exactly what mathematicians do.

steps.title: Mathematics = finding patterns and explaining them
steps.body:
Mathematics is, at its heart, the search for **patterns** and the **reasons** why they hold. Patterns appear in numbers, shapes, music, nature (petals, shells) and even in calendars.

Mathematics also helps us in science, technology, art and daily life — measuring, building, predicting weather, keeping time.

steps.title: The important sequences
steps.body:
A **sequence** is a list of numbers in order that follows a rule.

- All 1s: 1, 1, 1, 1, …
- Counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, …
- Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, …
- Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, …
- Triangular numbers: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, …
- Square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … (1×1, 2×2, 3×3 …)
- Cube numbers: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … (1×1×1, 2×2×2 …)
- Virahanka numbers: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … (each = sum of the two before it)
- Powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, … (keep doubling)
- Powers of 3: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81, … (keep tripling)

steps.title: Solved example 1 — find the rule
steps.body:
Find the next two terms: 2, 6, 18, 54, …

- Step 1: Look at differences: 4, 12, 36 — not constant.
- Step 2: Look at ratios: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, 18 ÷ 6 = 3, 54 ÷ 18 = 3. Each term is ×3.
- Step 3: 54 × 3 = 162, 162 × 3 = 486.
- Answer: **162, 486**

steps.title: Solved example 2 — Virahanka numbers
steps.body:
Continue 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …

- Rule: add the previous two terms.
- 8 + 13 = 21, 13 + 21 = 34, 21 + 34 = 55.
- Answer: **21, 34, 55**

The Indian scholar Virahanka studied these numbers while counting rhythms in poetry, centuries before they became known in Europe as Fibonacci numbers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking only the first two terms. 2, 4, … could be +2 (6 next) or ×2 (8 next). Always check several terms.
- Confusing square numbers (1, 4, 9) with even numbers (2, 4, 6).
- Forgetting that the triangular number jumps grow by 1 each time (+2, +3, +4 …).

quiz.why: Triangular numbers grow by +2, +3, +4, +5 and so on. After 15 comes a jump of +6, so the next number is 15 + 6 = 21.
A cube number is a number multiplied by itself three times. 64 = 4 × 4 × 4, while 100, 50 and 36 are not cubes.
In this sequence each term is the sum of the two before it, so the next term is 8 + 13 = 21. Doubling or adding a fixed number does not fit.
Powers of 3 multiply by 3 each time: 1, 3, 9, 27. So the next is 27 × 3 = 81.

options: the search for patterns and their explanations
quiz.why: Mathematics is about finding patterns and explaining why they work. It is not only tables, money or shapes.

scenes.text: Meena arranges ladoos in rows: 1 on top, 2 below, 3 below that.
The heap looks like a triangle — 6 ladoos, a triangular number.
Her brother arranges his in a 3 × 3 block — 9 ladoos, a square number.
Numbers have shapes!

steps.title: Triangular numbers as triangles
steps.body: Put dots in rows of 1, 2, 3, … The totals 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 make triangles. The nth triangular number = 1 + 2 + … + n.

steps.title: Square numbers as squares
steps.body: Arrange dots in an n × n grid: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. The nth square number = n × n.

steps.title: Cubes as stacks of cubes
steps.body: Small unit cubes stacked into a bigger cube of side n: 1, 8, 27, 64. The nth cube = n × n × n.

steps.title: Other pictures
steps.body:
- Odd numbers: an L-shape (a corner) of dots — 1, 3, 5, 7 dots.
- Powers of 2: each picture is two copies of the previous one.
- All 1s: a single dot each time.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
How many dots are in the 7th triangular picture?

- Step 1: 7th triangular number = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7.
- Step 2: Pair 1+6, 2+5, 3+4 = 7 each → 21, plus 7 = 28.
- Answer: **28 dots**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A square picture has 12 dots on each side row. How many dots in total?

- 12 × 12 = **144 dots**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the nth square has 2 × n dots. It has n × n dots (5th square is 25, not 10).
- In triangle pictures, forgetting the top row of 1 dot.

activity.prompt: Match the picture to the number.
pairs: L-shape with 4 dots on each arm, sharing a corner

quiz.q: A triangle of dots has 5 rows. How many dots?
quiz.why: A triangle with 5 rows has 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 dots. Adding row by row gives the total.
A square number is a number times itself. The 6th is 6 × 6 = 36.

quiz.q: An L-shaped corner picture shows which numbers?
quiz.why: An L-shaped corner adds 1, 3, 5, 7 dots, which are odd numbers. Adding each L to a square makes the next square.
The 3rd cube number is 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. 9 is the square, not the cube.

options: Each picture is two copies of the last
quiz.why: Each picture is made of two copies of the previous one, so the count doubles each time. That gives the powers of 2.

scenes.text: Teacher writes 1, 1+3, 1+3+5, 1+3+5+7 on the board.
Class adds: 1, 4, 9, 16.
'Those are square numbers!' shouts Riya.
Teacher shows how each odd L-shape wraps around a square to make the next square.

steps.title: Adding odd numbers gives squares
steps.body:
1 = 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9, 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 …

The sum of the first n odd numbers = **n × n**. Picture: each new odd number is an L-shape that wraps a square into the next bigger square.

steps.title: Adding up and down
steps.body:
1 + 2 + 1 = 4, 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 16.

Counting up to n and back down gives **n × n**. Picture: a square tilted on its corner, rows of dots counted diagonally.

steps.title: Two triangles make a square
steps.body: Add consecutive triangular numbers: 1 + 3 = 4, 3 + 6 = 9, 6 + 10 = 16. Two triangle pictures fit together into a square.

steps.title: More relations
steps.body:
- Adding powers of 2: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15, which is one less than 16. In general, the sum of powers of 2 up to a term is one less than the next power.
- Adding counting numbers and doubling: 2 × (1 + 2 + … + n) = n × (n + 1).
- Sums of cubes: 1, 1 + 8 = 9, 1 + 8 + 27 = 36 — these are squares of triangular numbers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 19 without adding one by one.

- Step 1: How many odd numbers? 19 is the 10th odd number ((19 + 1) ÷ 2 = 10).
- Step 2: Sum of first 10 odd numbers = 10 × 10.
- Answer: **100**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the number of odd numbers wrongly. Up to 19 there are 10 odd numbers, not 19 or 9.
- Using 'up and down' rule when the middle number is repeated — the peak is counted only once.

quiz.why: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n. Here there are 5 odd numbers, so 5 × 5 = 25.
3 + 6 = 9, which is 3 × 3, a square. Two neighbouring triangular numbers always add to a square.
1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31, which is one less than the next power of 2, 32. So the sum is 32 − 1 = 31.
Going up to 5 and back down to 1 gives 5 × 5 = 25. Adding 15 + 10 also gives 25.
1 + 8 + 27 = 36, which is the sum of the first three cubes. It also equals (1 + 2 + 3)² = 6 × 6.

scenes.text: Asha draws a triangle, then a square, then a pentagon in her rangoli.
Her cousin draws every line joining the dots on a circle.
They count sides and lines and find number sequences again!
Shapes and numbers are best friends.

steps.title: Shape sequences
steps.body:
- **Regular polygons**: triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, octagon, nonagon, decagon … Sides = 3, 4, 5, 6, … (counting numbers starting from 3).
- **Complete graphs**: dots on a circle with every pair joined. Lines for 2, 3, 4, 5 dots = 1, 3, 6, 10 — triangular numbers!
- **Stacked squares**: squares inside a square → square numbers.
- **Stacked triangles**: small triangles making a big triangle → 1, 4, 9, 16 small triangles (square numbers again).
- **Koch snowflake**: each side is replaced by 4 smaller pieces, so sides go 3, 12, 48, 192 (×4 each step).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
How many lines join 6 dots on a circle (complete graph)?

- Each dot joins to the other 5 → 6 × 5 = 30, but each line is counted twice.
- 30 ÷ 2 = **15 lines** (the 5th triangular number).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
The Koch snowflake starts with 3 sides. How many sides after 3 steps?

- Step 1: 3 × 4 = 12
- Step 2: 12 × 4 = 48
- Step 3: 48 × 4 = **192 sides**

steps.title: How to look for a pattern
steps.body: Count something in each shape (sides, corners, lines, small pieces), write the numbers as a list, then compare with the sequences you know.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting a line twice in complete graphs. Always divide by 2.
- Starting the polygon sequence from 1 or 2 sides — the smallest polygon has 3 sides.

activity.prompt: Which sequence does each pattern give?

items.text: Lines in complete graphs on 2, 3, 4, 5 dots
Squares of side 1, 2, 3 made from unit squares

quiz.q: How many sides does an octagon have?
quiz.why: 'Octa' means eight, so an octagon has 8 sides. A hexagon has 6.

quiz.q: Lines in a complete graph with 4 dots?
quiz.why: In a complete graph on 4 dots, each dot joins to 3 others. That counts each line twice, so 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6.

quiz.q: Stacked triangles with 4 rows contain how many small triangles?
quiz.why: Stacking triangle rows gives 1, 3, 5, 7 small triangles, so 4 rows hold 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. That is 4 × 4.

quiz.q: Koch snowflake sides multiply by … each step
quiz.why: In the Koch snowflake each side is replaced by 4 smaller sides, so the number of sides is multiplied by 4 each step.
The line counts 1, 3, 6, 10 follow the jumps +2, +3, +4, so they are triangular numbers. Squares and cubes grow differently.

questions.why: The squares go 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, so the next is 6 × 6 = 36. 49 is the square after 36.

questions.q: Which is NOT a triangular number?
questions.why: Triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21. 20 is not in the list, while 21, 10 and 15 are.

questions.q: Next power of 2 after 64?
questions.why: Powers of 2 double each time, so after 64 comes 64 × 2 = 128.

questions.q: 8th Virahanka number in 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …
questions.why: Each term is the sum of the two before it. The 8th term is 13 + 21 = 34.

questions.q: Sum of first 12 odd numbers?
questions.why: The sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n. For 12 odd numbers it is 12 × 12 = 144.

questions.q: Cube numbers: which comes after 125?
questions.why: Cubes go 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, and after 5³ = 125 comes 6³ = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16. Reason (R): The sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n.
options: Both true and R explains A
Both true but R does not explain A
questions.why: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 is true, and the sum of the first n odd numbers is n × n, which gives 4 × 4 = 16. So the reason explains the assertion.
Going up to 10 and back down to 1 gives 10 × 10 = 100. The same idea gave 25 for 5.
10 and 15 are neighbouring triangular numbers, and 10 + 15 = 25 = 5 × 5. So the sum is a square number.

questions.q: Lines in a complete graph on 7 dots?
questions.why: Each of 7 dots joins to 6 others, and each line is counted twice. So 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21.
1 + 2 + 4 + … + 512 is the sum of powers of 2 up to 512, which is one less than the next power, 1024. So it is 1023.

questions.q: Case: A shop stacks cans in a triangle: 1 on top, 2 below, and so on, with 12 rows. How many cans?
questions.why: The cans form 1 + 2 + … + 12 = 12 × 13 ÷ 2 = 78. 144 would be a square, not the sum.
The sum of the first four cubes is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4)² = 10² = 100. Check: 1 + 8 + 27 + 64 = 100.

questions.q: Koch snowflake after 4 steps (starting at 3 sides) has how many sides?
questions.why: Each step multiplies the number of sides by 4. From 3 sides: 3 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 768.

questions.q: Sum of the odd numbers from 21 to 39 (21 + 23 + … + 39)?
questions.why: Odd numbers from 21 to 39 = (sum of odd numbers up to 39) − (sum up to 19). The first 20 odd numbers sum to 20² = 400 and the first 10 sum to 10² = 100, so 400 − 100 = 300.

questions.q: Which statement is true?
options: Twice a triangular number is n × (n + 1)
questions.why: Twice a triangular number is n × (n + 1), because two copies of 1 + 2 + … + n fit into a rectangle n by n + 1. For example 2 × 6 = 3 × 4. Cubes can be even, squares can be odd, and Virahanka numbers add the previous two, not double.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Lines and Angles
courses.summary: Points, line segments, lines and rays; what an angle is; comparing angles; measuring angles in degrees with a protractor; drawing angles; and the types of angles — acute, right, obtuse, straight and reflex.
outcomes: Learners can name and draw points, line segments, lines and rays with correct notation
Learners can identify the vertex and arms of an angle and compare angles
Learners can measure and draw angles with a protractor
Learners can classify angles and solve problems on clock hands and turns

lessons.title: Point, line segment, line and ray

scenes.text: Dev shines a torch into the night sky. 'The light goes on and on!'
His mother stretches a thread between two nails: 'This one stops at both ends.'
A dot of ink marks a single spot — a point.
Dev now knows a ray, a line segment and a point from real life.

steps.title: The building blocks
steps.body:
- **Point**: an exact location; shown by a dot and named with a capital letter (P). It has no length or width.
- **Line segment**: the shortest path between two points; has two end-points; written AB with a bar on top. It has a fixed length.
- **Line**: a segment extended endlessly in both directions; written AB with arrows on both sides, or named with a small letter like l.
- **Ray**: starts at one point and goes on endlessly in one direction; written OA (start point first).

steps.title: Useful facts
steps.body:
- Through one point, infinitely many lines can pass.
- Through two points, exactly **one** line passes.
- Ray OA and ray AO are different rays (different starting points).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Name all line segments in a triangle PQR.

- Step 1: Pairs of corner points: P–Q, Q–R, R–P.
- Answer: **PQ, QR, RP** (3 segments)

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Four points A, B, C, D lie on one straight line in that order. How many line segments can be named?

- Pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD.
- Answer: **6 segments**

steps.title: Where you see them
steps.body: Edge of a ruler — segment. Railway track seen to the horizon — a model of a line. Sun's rays, torch beam — rays. Stars in the sky — points.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing ray AO when the ray starts at O — the start point always comes first.
- Saying a line has a length. Only a line segment can be measured.

activity.prompt: Match each object to the idea it models.

quiz.q: How many end-points does a ray have?
quiz.why: A ray starts at one end-point and goes on forever in one direction. So it has exactly 1 end-point.

quiz.q: How many lines pass through two given points?
quiz.why: Exactly one straight line can pass through two given points. That is why two points fix a line.

quiz.q: Which can be measured with a ruler?
quiz.why: A line segment has two end-points, so it has a fixed length that a ruler can measure. A ray and a line go on forever.
In the name of a ray, the first letter is the starting point. So ray PQ starts at P and passes through Q.

quiz.q: Points A, B, C on a line give how many segments?
quiz.why: Three points on a line give the segments AB, BC and AC. That is 3 segments.

lessons.title: What is an angle? Comparing angles

scenes.text: Riya opens the classroom door a little, then wider.
The door and the frame make an angle that grows as the door turns.
'Which opening is bigger?' asks the teacher.
The one where the door has turned more — the bigger angle.

steps.title: Angle
steps.body:
An **angle** is formed when two rays start from the same point. The common starting point is the **vertex**; the rays are the **arms**. Angle at vertex B between rays BA and BC is written ∠ABC (vertex letter in the middle) or ∠B.

An angle also measures **turning**: how much one arm has rotated from the other.

steps.title: Interior and exterior
steps.body: Points between the arms are in the **interior** of the angle; points outside are in the **exterior**.

steps.title: Comparing angles
steps.body:
- By superimposing: place one angle on the other with vertices and one arm together; the angle whose other arm lies outside is bigger.
- The length of the arms does **not** change the size of an angle — only the amount of turn matters.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
In ∠PQR, which point is the vertex?

- The middle letter names the vertex.
- Answer: **Q**; arms are QP and QR.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Three angles at O are formed by rays OA, OB, OC (OB between OA and OC). Name all angles.

- ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠AOC.
- Answer: **3 angles**, and ∠AOC = ∠AOB + ∠BOC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an angle drawn with longer arms is bigger. Size depends on turn, not arm length.
- Writing ∠PRQ for the angle at Q — the vertex must be in the middle.

statements.s: An angle with longer arms is always bigger.
The vertex is the common starting point of the arms.
∠ABC and ∠CBA are the same angle.
A point between the arms is in the exterior.

quiz.why: In an angle's name, the middle letter is the vertex. So in ∠XYZ the vertex is Y.

options: two rays with a common end-point
quiz.why: An angle is made by two rays that start from the same end-point, called the vertex. One ray or two parallel lines cannot make an angle.

quiz.q: Making the arms longer makes the angle …
quiz.why: The size of an angle depends only on how far one arm has turned from the other. Drawing longer arms does not change it.

quiz.q: With rays OA, OB, OC, OD from O (in order), how many angles?
quiz.why: Each angle uses a pair of the 4 rays. Choosing 2 from 4 gives 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = 6 angles.
An angle measures the amount of turning between its two arms. It is not area, weight or length.

scenes.text: At 3 o'clock, the clock hands make a corner like a book's corner.
Sana learns a full turn is divided into 360 equal parts called degrees.
She uses a protractor to measure the angle: 90°.
'So quarter turn = 90°!'

steps.title: Degrees
steps.body: A full turn is **360°**. Half turn = 180°, quarter turn = 90°. 1° is 1/360 of a full turn. The number 360 is old and convenient: it has many divisors (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 …).

steps.title: Using a protractor
steps.body:
- Place the centre of the protractor exactly on the vertex.
- Line up the base line (0° line) with one arm.
- Read where the other arm crosses the scale. Use the scale that starts at 0 on the arm you aligned (inner or outer).
- Check: if the angle looks smaller than a right angle, the answer must be less than 90°.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Through what angle does the minute hand turn in 20 minutes?

- Full turn (60 min) = 360°. 1 minute = 6°.
- 20 × 6 = **120°**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Angle between the hands at 4 o'clock?

- 12 hour marks → each gap = 360 ÷ 12 = 30°.
- From 12 to 4 = 4 gaps → **120°**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
You face North and turn clockwise to face South-East. How many degrees?

- N→E = 90°, E→SE = 45°. Total **135°**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the wrong scale (getting 130° instead of 50°). Check whether the angle looks acute or obtuse.
- Not placing the centre exactly at the vertex.

activity.prompt: How many degrees does the minute hand turn in 45 minutes?

quiz.why: A full turn brings you back to where you started, and that is 360°. 180° is half a turn and 90° is a quarter turn.

quiz.q: Angle between clock hands at 2 o'clock?
quiz.why: The clock face is 360° with 12 numbers, so each hour gap is 30°. At 2 o'clock the hands are 2 gaps apart: 2 × 30° = 60°.
A half turn is half of 360°, which is 180°. This is a straight line.
East and West point in opposite directions, so turning from one to the other is a half turn. That is 180°, whichever way you turn.

quiz.q: When using a protractor, its centre must be on …
quiz.why: The centre of the protractor must sit exactly on the vertex of the angle. Then one arm lines up with the zero line and the other arm gives the reading.

lessons.title: Types of angles and drawing angles

scenes.text: At the park, the slide makes a steep angle with the ground.
The school ramp is gentle — a small angle.
Kiran draws both in her notebook with a protractor.
She labels them: both acute, but the slide's is bigger.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Acute**: more than 0°, less than 90°
- **Right**: exactly 90° (a square corner, shown by a small square mark)
- **Obtuse**: more than 90°, less than 180°
- **Straight**: exactly 180° (arms in a line)
- **Reflex**: more than 180°, less than 360°
- **Complete**: 360°

Two lines that meet at a right angle are **perpendicular** (AB ⊥ CD).

steps.title: Drawing an angle of 65°
steps.body:
- Draw a ray BC.
- Place the protractor centre on B, base line along BC.
- Mark a point A at 65° on the scale starting from 0 at C.
- Join BA. ∠ABC = 65°.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Classify 35°, 90°, 145°, 180°, 250°.

- 35° acute, 90° right, 145° obtuse, 180° straight, **250° reflex**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A straight angle is split into two angles; one is 72°. Find the other.

- 180° − 72° = **108°** (obtuse).

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
The reflex angle at a point is 300°. What is the angle on the other side?

- 360° − 300° = **60°**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 90° acute or 180° obtuse. They are exactly right and exactly straight.
- Forgetting reflex angles: every angle smaller than 180° has a reflex partner (360° minus it).

quiz.why: An obtuse angle is bigger than 90° and smaller than 180°. 120° lies in that range, so it is obtuse.
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, which is 90°. 180° would make a straight line.

quiz.q: Other part of a straight angle if one part is 47°?
quiz.why: The two parts of a straight angle add to 180°. So the other part is 180° − 47° = 133°.
At 6 o'clock the two hands point in opposite directions, forming a straight line. So the angle is 180°.
A reflex angle is more than 180° but less than 360°. Angles below 90° are acute and between 90° and 180° obtuse.

questions.q: A line segment has how many end-points?
questions.why: A line segment is a part of a line with a start and an end. So it has 2 end-points.

questions.q: An angle of 90° is called …
questions.why: An angle of exactly 90° is called a right angle, like the corner of a book. Acute is below 90° and obtuse above it.

questions.q: Which notation names a ray starting at M?
questions.why: A ray is named with its starting point first, so a ray starting at M is ray MN. Ray NM would start at N.

questions.q: Angle between clock hands at 3 o'clock?
questions.why: Each hour gap on a clock is 30°. At 3 o'clock the hands are 3 gaps apart, 3 × 30° = 90°.

questions.q: Which is obtuse?
questions.why: An obtuse angle lies between 90° and 180°. 135° does, while 89° is acute, 90° is right and 185° is reflex.

questions.q: A quarter turn clockwise from North faces …
questions.why: A quarter turn is 90°. Going clockwise from North you meet East after 90°.

questions.q: How many angles are formed by 3 rays from one point (no ray overlapping)?
questions.why: Each angle uses a pair of the 3 rays, and choosing 2 from 3 gives 3 pairs. So there are 3 angles.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Making arms longer increases an angle. Reason (R): An angle measures the turn between arms.
questions.why: The assertion is false: longer arms do not change an angle, since the angle is the amount of turn between them. The reason is true, but it shows that A is wrong.

questions.q: Minute hand turns from 12 to 8. Angle turned?
questions.why: The minute hand moves 6° per minute (360° ÷ 60). From 12 to 8 is 40 minutes, so 40 × 6° = 240°.

questions.q: Reflex angle partner of 75°?
questions.why: The reflex angle partner is what is left of a full turn: 360° − 75° = 285°. Angles that add to 180° would give 105°, which is not the question.

questions.q: Two angles together make a straight angle; one is twice the other. Larger angle?
questions.why: A straight angle is 180°. If one angle is x and the other is 2x, then 3x = 180°, so x = 60° and the larger angle is 120°.

questions.q: Case: A ceiling fan blade turns 3 full rounds and a quarter. Total degrees?
questions.why: One full round is 360°, and a quarter round is 90°. So 3 × 360° + 90° = 1080° + 90° = 1170°.

questions.q: Smaller angle between clock hands at 9 o'clock?
questions.why: At 9 o'clock the hands are 3 hour-gaps apart on the shorter side. 3 × 30° = 90°, while 270° is the bigger angle.

questions.q: Points A, B, C, D, E lie on one line. Number of segments?
questions.why: Each pair of the 5 points gives one segment. So there are 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 segments.

questions.q: Smaller angle between hands at 2:30?
questions.why: At 2:30 the minute hand is at 180°, and the hour hand has moved halfway past 2, which is 60° + 15° = 75°. The difference is 180° − 75° = 105°.

questions.q: Facing West, Raju turns 270° anticlockwise. Now he faces …
questions.why: Anticlockwise from West: 90° gives South, 180° gives East and 270° gives North. So Raju faces North.

outcomes: Learners can reason about arrangements and 'supercells' in grids
Learners can explore digit sums, palindromes and reverse-and-add patterns
Learners can carry out Kaprekar's routine and the Collatz process
Learners can calculate mentally, estimate sensibly and find a winning strategy for simple number games

lessons.title: Numbers that tell us things · Supercells

scenes.text: Six friends stand in a line. Each calls out how many neighbours are taller than them.
They shout 0, 1, 2 — never more, because each has at most two neighbours.
Can everyone shout 2? No! The tallest person must say 0.
Numbers describe arrangements and also tell us what is impossible.

steps.title: Numbers as information
steps.body: In a line, a child can have at most 2 neighbours, so the number of taller neighbours is 0, 1 or 2. Whoever is tallest must say 0. Reasoning like this — what is possible, what is impossible — is real mathematics.

steps.title: Supercells
steps.body: In a grid of numbers, a cell is a **supercell** if its number is greater than all its neighbours (cells touching it on the left, right, above, below). Example row: 200 | 577 | 626 | 345 → 626 is a supercell in that row (greater than 577 and 345).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Row: 1 | 8 | 3 | 7 | 2 (neighbours only left/right). Find the supercells.

- 1: neighbour 8 → no. 8: neighbours 1, 3 → yes. 3: neighbours 8, 7 → no. 7: 3, 2 → yes. 2: neighbour 7 → no.
- Answer: **8 and 7**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Can every cell in a row be a supercell?

- If cell A is a supercell, A > its neighbour B, so B cannot be greater than A → B is not a supercell.
- So two neighbouring cells cannot both be supercells. Answer: **No**.

steps.title: Biggest number is always a supercell
steps.body: The largest number in a grid is bigger than everything, so it is always a supercell.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing with diagonal cells when the rule says only left, right, above, below.
- Forgetting edge cells have fewer neighbours.

statements.s: The largest number in a grid is always a supercell.
Two side-by-side cells can both be supercells.
statements.why: One must be larger than the other.

statements.s: In a line, a child can have 3 taller neighbours.
The smallest number can never be a supercell (unless it is alone).

quiz.why: A supercell is bigger than all its neighbours. 9 is bigger than 5 and 4, and 6 is bigger than 4 and 1, so 9 and 6 are supercells. 5, 4 and 1 each have a bigger neighbour.

quiz.q: In a line of children, the tallest says …
quiz.why: The tallest child has no taller neighbour, so the number of taller neighbours they report is 0.

quiz.q: Maximum number of supercells in a row of 5 cells?
quiz.why: Two neighbours cannot both be supercells, since one must be smaller. In a row of 5, alternate cells 1, 3 and 5 can be supercells, so the most is 3.
For supercells we compare with the cells that share an edge: left, right, above and below. Diagonal cells are not neighbours.
The largest number is bigger than every other number, so it must be bigger than its neighbours. So it is always a supercell.

scenes.text: Arjun spots a car number 4554 and says it reads the same backward.
He tries 47: 47 + 74 = 121 — another same-both-ways number!
His aunt calls these palindromes.
He starts collecting palindromes on his walks.

steps.title: Digit sums
steps.body:
Add the digits of a number: digit sum of 4,729 = 4 + 7 + 2 + 9 = 22.

Questions mathematicians ask: Which numbers have digit sum 14? What is the smallest 5-digit number with digit sum 1? (10,000)

steps.title: Palindromes
steps.body: A **palindrome** reads the same forwards and backwards: 66, 121, 4554, 12321. Words too: 'malayalam'.

steps.title: Reverse-and-add
steps.body:
Take a number, reverse its digits, add. Repeat until you get a palindrome.

- 47 + 74 = 121 ✓ (1 step)
- 68 + 86 = 154; 154 + 451 = 605; 605 + 506 = 1111 ✓ (3 steps)

Most numbers reach a palindrome quickly; for some numbers like 196 nobody yet knows if it ever happens.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Find the digit sum of the smallest 3-digit number and the largest 3-digit number.

- 100 → 1 + 0 + 0 = 1
- 999 → 9 + 9 + 9 = **27**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
How many 2-digit palindromes are there?

- They are 11, 22, …, 99 (both digits equal, first digit not 0).
- Answer: **9**

steps.title: Solved example 3
steps.body:
Count how many times the digit 7 appears when writing 1 to 100.

- Units place: 7, 17, …, 97 → 10 times.
- Tens place: 70–79 → 10 times.
- Answer: **20**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting 77 only once when counting digit 7 — it has two 7s.
- Calling 120 a palindrome; reversed it is 021, which is not the same.

activity.prompt: Reverse-and-add starting from 57: how many steps to a palindrome? (57+75=132, 132+231=363)

quiz.why: The digit sum is 3 + 0 + 5 + 0 + 8 = 16.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. 45654 does, while the others do not.
29 + 92 = 121, and 121 reads the same backwards, so it is a palindrome.
A 3-digit palindrome has the form aba. The first digit can be 1–9 (9 ways) and the middle digit 0–9 (10 ways), so 9 × 10 = 90.
A 4-digit number needs a non-zero first digit. With digit sum 1, the smallest is 1000, since 0001 is not 4-digit.

scenes.text: Teacher asks each student to pick a 4-digit number with not all digits equal.
They arrange digits biggest-first and smallest-first and subtract, again and again.
Everyone ends at 6174!
The routine is named after D. R. Kaprekar, an Indian maths teacher who discovered it.

steps.title: Kaprekar's routine
steps.body:
- Pick a 4-digit number whose digits are not all the same.
- Make the largest number from its digits and the smallest number from its digits.
- Subtract smaller from larger.
- Repeat with the answer (keep 4 digits, e.g. 999 → 0999).

You always reach **6174** within at most 7 steps, and then 7641 − 1467 = 6174 forever.

steps.title: Collatz conjecture
steps.body:
Start with any whole number. If even, halve it; if odd, multiply by 3 and add 1. Repeat.

It seems to always reach 1, but no one has proved it for all numbers yet — it is an **unsolved problem**. A guess like this is called a **conjecture**.

steps.title: Maths is still being made
steps.body: Problems like Collatz show maths is not finished. Anyone — even a student — can explore patterns that experts have not solved.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In Kaprekar's routine, dropping a leading 0 (treat 999 as 0999 → 9990 − 0999).
- In Collatz, doing 3n + 1 for even numbers. Only odd numbers get 3n + 1.

activity.prompt: Put Kaprekar's routine for 2111 in order.

quiz.why: Kaprekar's constant is 6174. Repeating 'largest minus smallest' on 4-digit numbers ends at 6174. 1729 is a different famous number.
In the Collatz rule, an odd number n becomes 3n + 1. For 7: 3 × 7 + 1 = 22.
In the Collatz rule, an even number is halved. 40 ÷ 2 = 20.

options: a guess believed true but not yet proved
quiz.why: A conjecture is a statement believed to be true but not yet proved. If proved it becomes a theorem, and a wrong one is not a conjecture.
7641 − 1467 = 6174, since 7641 is the largest and 1467 the smallest arrangement of the digits 6, 1, 7, 4. Repeating the routine on 6174 gives 6174 again.

lessons.title: Mental maths, estimation and number games

scenes.text: Neha buys items costing ₹198, ₹302 and ₹49.
Her friend estimates: about 200 + 300 + 50 = 550.
Later they play the '21 game' and Neha finds a sure way to win.

steps.title: Estimation
steps.body: Round numbers to make a quick, sensible guess. How many hours in a year? 365 × 24 ≈ 365 × 25 = 9125 → about 9,000 (exactly 8,760). Estimates check whether an exact answer is reasonable.

steps.title: Winning strategy — the 21 game
steps.body:
Two players say numbers in turn, adding 1 or 2 to the last number, starting from 0; whoever says 21 wins.

- Work backwards: say 21 → you need to say 18 before (opponent can only reach 19 or 20) → so also 15, 12, 9, 6, 3.
- Say the multiples of 3 and you always win.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Estimate 48 × 52.

- ≈ 50 × 50 = 2,500. Exact: 2,496. Estimate is close.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding and forgetting to adjust back (999 + 457 is not 1457).
- Treating an estimate as the exact answer in a question that asks for the exact value.

a.text: 21 game: you may add 1 or 2; target 21. Your friend just said 4. What do you say?

choices.label: Say 5
choices.feedback: 5 is not a multiple of 3 — your friend can reach 6.

choices.label: Say 6
choices.feedback: 6 is a multiple of 3. Now you control the game.

b.text: Your friend says 6 and keeps saying multiples of 3. They reach 21 first.

c.text: Whatever your friend says (7 or 8), you jump to 9, then 12, 15, 18 and 21. You win!

quiz.why: 297 is 3 less than 300 and 503 is 3 more than 500, so the changes cancel. 300 + 500 = 800.
61 is close to 60 and 39 is close to 40. So 61 × 39 is about 60 × 40 = 2,400.

quiz.q: In the 21 game (add 1 or 2), the safe numbers are multiples of …
quiz.why: If you reach a multiple of 3, the opponent adds 1 or 2 and you can add 2 or 1 to reach the next multiple. So you keep landing on multiples of 3 up to 21.
A week has 7 days and each day has 24 hours. So 7 × 24 = 168 hours.

questions.q: Digit sum of 9,081?
questions.why: The digit sum of 9,081 is 9 + 0 + 8 + 1 = 18.

questions.q: Which is a palindrome?
questions.why: A palindrome reads the same in both directions. 10101 does, while 12312, 21010 and 10110 do not.

questions.q: Collatz: next after 9?
questions.why: 9 is odd, so the Collatz rule gives 3 × 9 + 1 = 28.

questions.q: Supercells in row 3 | 1 | 5 | 2 | 8 (left/right neighbours only)?
questions.why: Compare each number with its left and right neighbours. 3 > 1, 5 > 1 and 2, and 8 > 2, so 3, 5 and 8 are supercells. 1 and 2 each have a bigger neighbour.
38 + 83 = 121, which is a palindrome.

questions.q: Estimate 498 × 21.
questions.why: 498 is about 500 and 21 is about 20. So 500 × 20 = 10,000 is a good estimate.

questions.q: Kaprekar step: 6543 → ?
questions.why: A Kaprekar step arranges the digits to make the largest and smallest numbers and subtracts. For 6543 that is 6543 − 3456 = 3087.

questions.q: How many times is the digit 5 written from 1 to 60?
questions.why: In the units place, 5 appears in 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, which is 6 times. In the tens place, 50 to 59 gives 10 more, so 6 + 10 = 16.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Neighbouring cells cannot both be supercells. Reason (R): Of two different numbers, one is larger.
options: Both true, R doesn't explain A
questions.why: Both are true: neighbouring numbers differ, so one is larger. The smaller one then cannot be bigger than all its neighbours, so both cannot be supercells.

questions.q: Collatz from 12 reaches 1 after how many steps? (12→6→3→10→5→16→8→4→2→1)
questions.why: The sequence 12→6→3→10→5→16→8→4→2→1 has 9 arrows, so there are 9 steps.

questions.q: Largest 5-digit number with digit sum 10?
questions.why: To make the largest number, put the biggest digits in front. With sum 10 that is 9, then 1, then zeros: 91000.

questions.q: Case: In the 21 game (start at 0, add 1 or 2 each turn, whoever says 21 wins), which numbers should you aim to say to be sure of winning?
questions.why: From a multiple of 3, the opponent can only reach the next two numbers, and you can always jump to the next multiple of 3, ending at 21.

questions.q: Smallest number of steps for 2111 to reach 6174 (Kaprekar)?
questions.why: The steps are 2111 → 0999 → 8991 → 8082 → 8532 → 6174. That is 5 steps of 'largest minus smallest'.

questions.q: Reverse-and-add from 89 takes many steps. Which does 89 + 98 give?
questions.why: 89 + 98 = 187, which is not a palindrome yet. So the reverse-and-add must continue.

questions.q: Mental: 25 × 48 = ?
Exactly how many hours are there in a non-leap year?
questions.why: A non-leap year has 365 days, each with 24 hours. So 365 × 24 = 8,760 hours.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Data Handling and Presentation
courses.summary: Collecting and organising data, tally marks and frequency tables, pictographs with a key, reading and drawing bar graphs with a sensible scale, and interpreting graphs honestly.
outcomes: Learners can collect data and organise it with tally marks in a frequency table
Learners can read and draw pictographs using a key
Learners can read, draw and choose a scale for bar graphs
Learners can draw conclusions from data and spot misleading graphs

scenes.text: Class 6B must choose a picnic spot: zoo, lake, fort or museum.
Every student writes one choice on a slip.
Monitor Asha sorts the slips using tally marks.
The table shows the lake wins with 14 votes.

steps.title: Data
steps.body: **Data** is a collection of facts — numbers, words or measurements — gathered to answer a question. First decide the question, then collect, then organise.

steps.title: Tally marks and frequency
steps.body:
Draw a stroke | for each item; every 5th stroke crosses the previous four (卌 style bundle). Bundles of 5 make counting fast.

The number of times an item occurs is its **frequency**. A table with items, tallies and frequencies is a **frequency table**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A tally shows 卌 卌 |||. What is the frequency?

- Two bundles of 5 = 10, plus 3 = **13**

steps.title: Always check totals
steps.body: The sum of frequencies must equal the number of observations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Making bundles of 4 or 6 instead of 5.
- Losing or double-counting items — cross each one off as you tally.

activity.prompt: Tally: 卌 卌 卌 ||. Frequency?

quiz.q: Each bundle of tally marks stands for …
quiz.why: Tally marks are made in bundles of five, with the fifth stroke crossing the four. So each bundle stands for 5.

options: how many times a value occurs
quiz.why: Frequency is the number of times a value occurs in the data. It is not the average or the largest value.
The total is the sum of the frequencies: 4 + 7 + 3 + 6 = 20.
We first decide what question we want to answer, since that tells what data to collect. Drawing and colouring come later.
A bundle of five is 5, and the four strokes beside it are 4. So 5 + 4 = 9.

scenes.text: The canteen sells apples, bananas, oranges each day.
The manager draws one 🍎 picture for every 10 fruits sold.
A half picture means 5.
Parents can see at a glance which fruit is popular.

steps.title: Pictograph
steps.body: A **pictograph** shows data with pictures or symbols. A **key** (scale) tells what one symbol stands for, e.g. 🍎 = 10 apples. Part symbols (half a picture) show part values.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Key: 🙂 = 4 students. Cricket row shows 🙂🙂🙂🙂🙂 and half 🙂. How many like cricket?

- 5 full × 4 = 20; half = 2.
- Answer: **22 students**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Show 35 books with key 📘 = 10 books.

- 35 ÷ 10 = 3.5 → **3 full symbols and half a symbol**.

steps.title: Choosing a key
steps.body: Pick a key that keeps the number of symbols small but easy: if data are 120, 80, 150, use 1 symbol = 10 or 20 (not 1, which needs 150 pictures).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the key and counting symbols as the answer.
- Using different-sized symbols — every symbol must be the same size so rows compare fairly.

activity.prompt: Key: ⭐ = 6 points. Match rows to totals.

quiz.why: Each symbol stands for 5, so 7 symbols stand for 7 × 5 = 35.
Each symbol stands for 8, so 20 needs 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 symbols. That is 2 full symbols and a half.

quiz.q: Why do pictographs need a key?
options: to tell what one symbol stands for
quiz.why: The key tells what one symbol stands for. Without it, the reader cannot work out the values.
A half symbol is half of 100, which is 50.

options: Hard to show exact odd values
quiz.why: A pictograph cannot easily show exact odd values, because drawing fractions of pictures exactly is hard. It can still compare and does use a key.

scenes.text: Farmer Ramesh sees a bar graph of monthly rainfall at the panchayat office.
July's bar is the tallest; March's is tiny.
He reads the scale: 1 unit = 50 mm.
He plans his sowing for the rainy months.

steps.title: Bar graph
steps.body: A **bar graph** uses bars of equal width with equal gaps between them. The **length/height** shows the value. One axis lists categories; the other has a number scale (e.g. 1 unit = 10).

steps.title: How to read
steps.body:
- Read the title and axis labels.
- Check the scale.
- For each bar, read where its top meets the scale.
- Compare: tallest = most, shortest = least; difference = subtract values.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Scale: 1 unit = 20 students. Bars: Hindi 4 units, English 3 units, Maths 5 units.

- Hindi 80, English 60, Maths 100.
- Maths has **20 more** students than Hindi.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
A bar reaches halfway between 40 and 50 on the scale. Value?

- Halfway = **45**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the number of grid boxes instead of multiplying by the scale.
- Comparing bars without checking that both graphs use the same scale.

statements.s: All bars in a bar graph must have the same width.
Gaps between bars must be equal.
A wider bar means a bigger value.
A bar graph needs a scale.

quiz.q: Scale 1 unit = 5. Bar is 7 units. Value?
quiz.why: Each unit stands for 5, so a bar of 7 units shows 7 × 5 = 35.
The tallest bar shows the greatest value, since height shows the value. The shortest shows the least.
The difference is 120 − 75 = 45.

quiz.q: In a bar graph, what shows the value?
quiz.why: In a bar graph, the length (height) of the bar shows the value. The colour and gap do not.
Halfway between 200 and 300 is (200 + 300) ÷ 2 = 250.

lessons.title: Drawing bar graphs and interpreting data

scenes.text: Zoya counts vehicles at a crossing for an hour.
Cars 120, bikes 180, buses 30, autos 90.
She chooses a scale 1 unit = 30 so bars fit on her page.
Her graph helps the RWA ask for a zebra crossing.

steps.title: Steps to draw
steps.body:
- Draw two perpendicular axes; label them.
- Mark categories at equal gaps on one axis.
- Choose a scale based on the largest value and the paper size.
- Draw bars of equal width to the right heights.
- Give a title.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Data: 120, 180, 30, 90. Choose a scale for a 10-unit-tall page.

- Largest = 180. 180 ÷ 10 = 18 → choose a neat 20 per unit (9 units) or 30 per unit (6 units).
- With 1 unit = 30: bars are 4, 6, 1, 3 units.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Interpret: which vehicle type is half the bikes?

- Bikes 180 → half = 90 → **autos**.

steps.title: Misleading graphs
steps.body: If the number axis does not start at 0, small differences can look huge. Always check the scale. Infographics should be eye-catching but honest.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Uneven scale steps (0, 10, 30, 40) — steps must be equal.
- Forgetting title or labels — a graph without them is meaningless.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to draw a bar graph.
items: Decide what to show and collect data
Draw and label the two axes
Draw bars of equal width to correct heights

quiz.q: Largest value 480, 8 units available. Good scale?
quiz.why: With 1 unit = 60, the largest value 480 needs 480 ÷ 60 = 8 units, exactly what is available. A scale of 10 would need 48 units.

quiz.q: A graph's number axis starts at 90. Risk?
quiz.why: If the axis starts at 90 instead of 0, small differences look much bigger. This can mislead the reader.
The steps on a scale must be equal, so each gap means the same amount. Uneven steps would distort the graph.

quiz.q: With 1 unit = 30, value 150 needs a bar of …
quiz.why: With 1 unit = 30, a value of 150 needs 150 ÷ 30 = 5 units.
Every graph should have a title and labelled axes so readers know what it shows. Colours and 3D bars are not essential.

questions.q: Tally 卌 卌 | represents …
questions.why: Each full bundle is 5, so two bundles are 10, and the single stroke adds 1. So 5 + 5 + 1 = 11.

questions.q: Pictograph key 🌸 = 3. Row has 4 🌸. Value?
questions.why: Each symbol stands for 3, so 4 symbols stand for 4 × 3 = 12.

questions.q: In a bar graph, bars must have …
questions.why: In a bar graph the bars have equal widths, so only their lengths differ. Different widths could mislead the reader.

questions.q: Frequencies: red 7, blue 9, green 4. Most popular?
questions.why: The most popular colour has the highest frequency. Blue has 9, which is more than red's 7 and green's 4.

questions.q: Scale 1 unit = 25. Bar of 6 units = ?
questions.why: Each unit is 25, so 6 units give 6 × 25 = 150.

questions.q: Key 🐄 = 20. To show 70, draw …
questions.why: Each symbol is 20, so 70 needs 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5 symbols, that is 3 and a half.

questions.q: Values 35, 60, 15, 90. Best scale for about 9 units?
questions.why: The largest value is 90. With 1 unit = 10 it takes 9 units, which is about right. 1 unit = 100 would be too big and 1 unit = 1 too small.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Graph A shows a bar twice as tall as another, so its value is double. Reason (R): The number axis starts at 50.
options: Both true and R explains A
A may be false; R explains why the picture misleads
questions.why: If the axis starts at 50 and not 0, the heights are not proportional to the values. So a bar twice as tall may not mean double, and the reason explains why the picture misleads.

questions.q: Case: Library book issues: Mon 40, Tue 55, Wed 30, Thu 75, Fri 50. Total?
Using the same data, how many more on Thu than the average of Mon and Wed?
questions.why: The average of Mon and Wed is (40 + 30) ÷ 2 = 35. Thursday has 75, so it is 75 − 35 = 40 more.

questions.q: A tally for 23 has how many full bundles?
questions.why: Each bundle is 5, and 4 × 5 = 20. The other 3 are loose strokes, so there are 4 full bundles.

questions.q: Case: A pictograph with key 🧃 = 12 shows juice sales: 5½ symbols. Sales?
questions.why: Each symbol is 12, so 5 symbols are 60, and a half symbol is 6. So 60 + 6 = 66.

questions.q: Frequencies of 4 items add to 50. Three are 12, 15, 9. Fourth?
questions.why: The three known frequencies add to 12 + 15 + 9 = 36. The fourth is 50 − 36 = 14.

questions.q: Which is NOT a good reason to use a bar graph?
questions.why: Bar graphs compare quantities and show largest and smallest, such as survey results. Showing exact pictures of objects is what pictographs do.

questions.q: Case: Two graphs show the same data; graph P uses 1 unit = 10, graph Q uses 1 unit = 20. A value of 80 appears as …
questions.why: Units = value ÷ scale. In P, 80 ÷ 10 = 8 units, and in Q, 80 ÷ 20 = 4 units. So the same value looks shorter on Q.

questions.q: Scores 48, 72, 36, 60 drawn with 1 unit = 12. Total bar length?

courses.title: Ch 5 · Prime Time
courses.summary: Multiples and factors, common multiples and common factors, prime and composite numbers, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, co-prime numbers, prime factorisation, and divisibility tests.
outcomes: Learners can list factors and multiples and find common ones
Learners can identify primes and composites and use the sieve
Learners can test whether two numbers are co-prime
Learners can write the prime factorisation of a number and use divisibility tests

scenes.text: The class counts 1, 2, 3… Multiples of 3 say 'idli', multiples of 5 say 'vada'.
At 15, Ravi must say 'idli-vada' — it is a multiple of both!
Next 'idli-vada' is 30, then 45.
These are the common multiples of 3 and 5.

steps.title: Factors and multiples
steps.body:
If a × b = n, then a and b are **factors** of n, and n is a **multiple** of a and of b.

- Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (finitely many)
- Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, … (infinitely many)
- 1 is a factor of every number; every number is a factor and a multiple of itself.

steps.title: Common multiples and factors
steps.body:
- **Common multiples** of 4 and 6: 12, 24, 36 … (the smallest is 12).
- **Common factors** of 12 and 18: 1, 2, 3, 6 (the largest is 6).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Two lights blink every 4 s and every 6 s. Both blink now. When next together?

- Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, …
- Multiples of 6: 6, 12, …
- Answer: after **12 seconds**

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Find common factors of 24 and 36.

- Factors of 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24
- Factors of 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36
- Common: **1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12**

steps.title: Find factors in pairs
steps.body: For 36: 1×36, 2×18, 3×12, 4×9, 6×6. Stop when the pair repeats.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up factor (divides into) and multiple (times table).
- Forgetting 1 and the number itself in the factor list.

activity.prompt: Is it a common multiple of 4 and 6?

quiz.why: Factors of 18 come in pairs: 1 × 18, 2 × 9 and 3 × 6. So they are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24 and of 8 are 8, 16, 24. The smallest common one is 24.
